items.title: Crisis en Ceuta
items.summary: Una particular hace una parte del trabajo que, casi una semana después de la llegada masiva de migrantes, todavía no han asumido los servicios sociales de la ciudad autónoma ni los del Gobierno central
items.body_text:
- Directo Última hora sobre la crisis migratoria en Ceuta
- Crisis migratoria La Guardia Civil busca a los 6.000 inmigrantes que "deambulan" por Ceuta para devolverlos por la fuerza a Marruecos
Cada mañana, a las nueve, Sabah abre la puerta de su casa. No vuelve a cerrarla hasta cerca de las 11 de la noche. A veces, incluso más tarde. Por esa puerta pasan hasta 400 personas al día. Su vivienda de Los Rosales se ha convertido en comedor social, almacén de ropa para inmigrantes, baño público, oficina de búsqueda de desaparecidos y refugio para menores. Una casa particular está haciendo una parte del trabajo que, casi una semana después de la llegada masiva de migrantes a Ceuta, todavía no han asumido los servicios sociales de la ciudad autónoma ni los del Gobierno central.
Sabah es empresaria de bazares y comparte normalmente las dos plantas y la terraza del edificio con su marido, su hijo y una sobrina. «Cuando estalló todo esto se fueron de vacaciones y me dejaron aquí a lo mío», cuenta. Ahora, sus habitaciones sirven de refugio para niñas vulnerables y de almacén para bolsas de ropa, cajas de comida y perolas. También reciben a personas que necesitan comer, lavarse, vestirse o encontrar a sus seres queridos.
No está sola. Una red de mujeres musulmanas de Los Rosales, El Príncipe y La Reina cocina durante horas, clasifica prendas, reúne productos de higiene y busca un lugar seguro para quienes duermen en la calle. Los vecinos aportan alimentos, dinero y vehículos. Algunas familias abren sus casas. «Los productos son donaciones de vecinos, empresarios locales e incluso niños que han vaciado sus huchas», cuenta emocionada.
En la terraza, varias mujeres remueven un estofado de carne picada dentro de grandes perolas. Otras llenan recipientes que después se reparten en la calle. La actividad no se detiene. «Ayer entregamos unas 200 y pico raciones», calcula Sabah. «Pero luego está la gente que estaba escondida en los campos y que viene por la tarde para ducharse y comer. Han pasado unas 400 y pico personas».
Los hombres y los niños se lavan al aire libre en la azotea. Suben en pequeños grupos con la ropa dentro de bolsas de basura. No hay duchas ni vestuarios. Se asean con cubos, barreños y recipientes de plástico, mientras los voluntarios reponen el agua y reparten jabón. Las mujeres utilizan los baños de las plantas inferiores para conservar su intimidad. Algunos migrantes, después de recibir comida o ropa, se quedan para ayudar a quienes continúan esperando.
Las camas de la vivienda han desaparecido bajo bolsas, barras de pan, latas, ropa, paquetes de macarrones... Lo que antes era una casa es ahora un centro logístico. ¿Qué es lo que más cuesta encontrar? «Ropa interior», responde ella. «Mi hija fue a Algeciras a recoger varios paquetes que enviaron unas amigas de Gibraltar y he regalado los calzoncillos de mi marido y mis hijos... Verás cuando vuelvan», cuenta riendo.
Su prioridad, sin embargo, son los menores. Especialmente, las niñas. Cuatro llegaron sin previo aviso esta madrugada. La víspera, le despertó el timbre: otras tres entraron «con la ropa desgarrada y pidiendo auxilio». El relato de Sabah coincide con lo que otros vecinos ya contaron a este diario: algunas de menores que vagan solas por Ceuta han sufrido abusos o situaciones de explotación sexual.
«Yo no quiero tener a nadie durmiendo», comienza. Después se interrumpe: «Pero cuando ves un intento de violación...». Las niñas duermen donde pueden, dentro de las habitaciones de una familia que no conocían antes de cruzar la frontera. «Ayer, estaban como sardinas en lata», afirma.
La violencia sexual contra las chicas es uno de los problemas que más preocupa a los habitantes de estas barriadas. items.body_text:
Castilla-La Mancha supera los 5.700 casos activos de violencia de género en el sistema VioGén
La comunidad registra 5.776 mujeres protegidas por el sistema de seguimiento policial del Ministerio del Interior, que contabiliza más de 104.600 casos activos en toda España
J. Guayerbas
Toledo
Castilla-La Mancha mantiene 5.776 casos activos de violencia de género en el sistema VioGén, la herramienta del Ministerio del Interior para el seguimiento y protección de las víctimas. La cifra, actualizada a 31 de julio, sitúa a la región entre las comunidades autónomas ... con mayor número de mujeres incluidas en este sistema.
En el conjunto del país permanecen activos 104.666 casos, de los que 1.165 presentan un nivel de riesgo alto y 14 están clasificados como de riesgo extremo, según los últimos datos publicados por el Ministerio del Interior.
La estadística pone de manifiesto, además, el impacto de la violencia machista sobre los menores. De los expedientes activos, 53.818 corresponden a víctimas con hijos a su cargo, mientras que en 1.664 casos los menores se encuentran también en situación de riesgo. De ellos, 149 están considerados de riesgo alto y tres de riesgo extremo.
Noticia relacionada
- 
Antonio González Jerez
Por franjas de edad, las mujeres de entre 31 y 45 años concentran el mayor número de casos activos, con 48.357, seguidas por las de 18 a 30 años (25.756) y las de 46 a 64 años (26.685). El sistema también incluye 1.335 víctimas menores de edad y 2.533 de 65 años o más.
Indicadores de riesgo letal
Interior identifica igualmente 13.464 casos de especial relevancia, una categoría reservada para aquellas situaciones en las que concurren indicadores que incrementan de forma significativa el riesgo de que el agresor pueda ejercer una violencia muy grave o incluso letal.
Por comunidades autónomas, Andalucía continúa siendo la que acumula un mayor número de casos activos, con 27.885, por delante de la Comunidad Valenciana (17.111) y la Comunidad de Madrid (12.591). Castilla-La Mancha, con 5.776 casos, ocupa la séptima posición del país, por encima de Murcia (5.733) y Castilla y León (5.586).

items.body_text:
Investigado por el fuego de Berrocal (Salamanca) tras cortar con una radial
El fuego, originado mientras realizaba una actividad prohibida durante la época de alto riesgo de incendios, calcinó unas 214 hectáreas de pasto
H. D.
Valladolid
La Guardia Civil investiga a un varón como presunto autor de un delito de incendio forestal por imprudencia grave tras el fuego declarado el pasado 28 de julio en el término municipal de Berrocal de Huebra (Salamanca).
La investigación apunta a que el incendio se ... originó mientras el investigado realizaba trabajos de corte con una radial en una finca, una actividad expresamente prohibida en ese momento debido a la situación de alto riesgo de incendios forestales en Castilla y León.
Tras conocer los hechos, agentes del Servicio de Protección de la Naturaleza (SEPRONA) de Béjar llevaron a cabo la correspondiente inspección técnico-ocular en la zona afectada, además de identificar a las personas presentes y tomar declaración a posibles testigos.
Noticia relacionada
Como resultado de las pesquisas, determinaron que el origen del fuego se encontraba en unos trabajos realizados con una radial en la plaza de toros situada dentro de la finca. La utilización de esta maquinaria estaba prohibida al encontrarse el lugar dentro de la zona de monte y de su franja de protección de 400 metros, además de estar vigente una alerta por riesgo meteorológico de incendios forestales.
El incendio fue declarado inicialmente con un Índice de Gravedad Potencial 1 (IGR-1), al existir riesgo de afección para la población y diversas infraestructuras, aunque posteriormente fue rebajado a IGR-0 al descartarse esas circunstancias. Sin embargo, las llamas se reactivaron durante la jornada del 29 de julio y terminaron afectando a una superficie aproximada de 214 hectáreas de pasto.
Tres personas afectadas
Como consecuencia del incendio, tres personas resultaron afectadas. Dos de ellas sufrieron quemaduras leves en brazos y piernas, mientras que una tercera tuvo que ser atendida por inhalación de humo. Además, el fuego alcanzó una cabaña ganadera en la que murieron alrededor de 80 ovejas.
La Guardia Civil recuerda que entre el 12 de junio y el 12 de octubre permanece declarada la época de peligro alto de incendios forestales en Castilla y León, periodo durante el que está prohibido utilizar determinadas herramientas y maquinaria capaces de generar chispas o focos de ignición en el monte y en su zona de influencia.
En lo que va de campaña, la Comandancia de Salamanca ha investigado ya a cinco personas por delitos de incendio forestal cometidos por imprudencia grave relacionados con el uso de desbrozadoras, radiales y quemas agrícolas, además de haber detenido a otra persona como presunta autora de un incendio intencionado. Asimismo, la Guardia Civil insistió en la importancia de respetar las medidas de prevención y recordó que la colaboración ciudadana resulta fundamental para evitar este tipo de sucesos y proteger el patrimonio natural.

items.body_text:
El Gobierno transfiere casi 6,5 millones de euros a Ceuta para «reforzar» la atención a inmigrantes
Esta partida se busca «reforzar» todos los mecanismos de ayuda y acogida disponibles y «garantizar la atención sociosanitaria» de los migrantes que se encuentran tanto en el Centro de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes (CETI)
El Ministerio de Inclusión, Seguridad Social y Migraciones ha realizado una transferencia de crédito extraordinario de casi 6,5 millones de euros a Ceuta.
Según han informado fuentes del departamento que dirige Elma Saiz, con esta partida se busca «reforzar» todos los mecanismos de ... ayuda y acogida disponibles y «garantizar la atención sociosanitaria» de los inmigrantes que se encuentran tanto en el Centro de Estancia Temporal de Inmigrantes (CETI) y en sus aledaños, con «especial prioridad para quienes se encuentran en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad».
Asimismo, el Ministerio ha subrayado que las medidas que se están llevando a cabo para reforzar la red de acogida han permitido ampliar en 72 plazas el CETI de Ceuta, una ampliación que «se ha hecho efectiva gracias a la colaboración del Ministerio del Interior y Ministerio de Defensa, que ha trasladado material disponible desde el Centro de Acogida Las Raíces de Tenerife».
Noticia relacionada
El Ministerio también ha destacado que ha concertado con Cruz Roja la atención sociosanitaria de los inmigrantes que permanecen en la playa y en los alrededores del CETI, distribuyendo kits de alimentación.
La ministra Elma Saiz participa este jueves de forma telemática en un encuentro de coordinación del dispositivo de atención humanitaria en la Delegación del Gobierno de Ceuta, junto a la secretaria de Estado de Migraciones, Pilar Cancela.
Inclusión ha asegurado que sigue «muy de cerca» la situación en Ceuta y que se ha mantenido «desde el primer momento en permanente contacto y coordinación» con el Gobierno de la Ciudad Autónoma, con la Delegación del Gobierno en Ceuta, el Ministerio del Interior y con el resto de las administraciones implicadas, para «dar una respuesta humanitaria adecuada, coordinada y eficaz ante esta situación extraordinaria»

items.title: Abdul El‑Sayed, a progressive, wins Michigan Senate Democratic primary in key battle for party’s future
items.summary: Critical of Israel and a proponent of universal public healthcare, the contender scored a narrow victory in the swing state after an all‑night count
items.body_text:
Abdul El‑Sayed, a progressive, wins Michigan Senate Democratic primary in key battle for party’s future
Critical of Israel and a proponent of universal public healthcare, the contender scored a narrow victory in the swing state after an all‑night count
Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens with 48.5% of the vote, both CNN and the Associated Press reported, calling it “a massive victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state.” The close race reflects how divided the party is, as well as the rise of a leftist wing that demands change.
The 41‑year‑old physician, the son of Egyptian immigrants and a representative of the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, has landed a blow in the debate over the future of Democratic opposition to Donald Trump by defeating Haley Stevens, who had the backing of the party’s heavyweights as well as special interest groups. El-Sayed’s campaign said Stevens called to concede Wednesday, according to AP.
The vote shows that the rise of young left‑wing (and even self-styled socialist) politicians is not confined to liberal strongholds. The wave that Zohran Mamdani began last year with his win in New York has spread to a swing state like Michigan, where either Republicans or Democrats can hold sway. El‑Sayed’s victory confirms that the party of Barack Obama and Joe Biden is entering a new era in which the old rules no longer apply.
The hardest part still lies ahead for El‑Sayed. After beating the centrist Stevens, he will have to prove in November that a candidate like himself — a Muslim and a proponent of ideas that were until recently viewed as radical — can defeat the Republican candidate in the midterm elections. If he were to succeed, he would become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history and join figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders, Representative Alexandria Ocasio‑Cortez and Mayor Mamdani on the list of leaders changing the face of the Democratic Party.
El‑Sayed does not describe himself as a socialist, but he champions causes largely associated with the left. He rose to prominence in Michigan on platforms such as ending unconditional U.S. aid to Israel — which he accuses openly of genocide in Gaza — and advancing universal public healthcare. He combines that message with a personal magnetism, and is often seen wearing a fitted black T‑shirt in videos that show him lifting weights in a gym or dancing in a cowboy hat to Taylor Swift’s You Belong With Me. His campaign team likely studied how Mamdani’s videos went viral during the run that elected him New York mayor last year. Now another progressive has once again found the formula to win over voters.
With this victory, El‑Sayed has defeated the party establishment in Michigan, led by Governor Gretchen Whitmer and Senator Gary Peters, who backed his rival. He has also challenged the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a lobby that spent about $30 million on this race — the largest sum ever poured into a single contest. It appears to have had little effect.
Accusation of antisemitism
In the final stretch of the campaign, Representative Stevens made a tentative charge of antisemitism against El‑Sayed — “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans” — and accused him of seeking only “fame and, probably, money” in his political career. But it was already too late. El‑Sayed had managed to establish himself as a breath of fresh air, someone who cares about people’s real problems and about ending the influence of dark money in elections, in contrast to the old style of politics Stevens represented.
Primaries were held Tuesday in states including Virginia, Missouri, Kansas, and Washington. But all eyes were on Michigan, perhaps the most consequential contest ahead of the elections that will define the second half of Trump’s term. Attention was intense for several reasons. items.summary: The former agency counterterrorism chief of operations and Cuban exile is convinced Washington is preparing a decisive blow against the island’s regime

Ric Prado, ex-CIA officer: ‘Cuba is the next apple to fall from the tree’
The former agency counterterrorism chief of operations and Cuban exile is convinced Washington is preparing a decisive blow against the island’s regime
Enrique “Ric” Prado is 75, his voice measured from having told this story many times and from an uncomfortable habit: saying in public things most people with his résumé prefer to keep to themselves. He retired from the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) in 2004 with a rank equivalent to a two-star general after 24 years of service and, he says, as the first Hispanic officer with paramilitary credentials in the department. He now lives quietly, devoted to his family and giving talks about the memoir he published in 2022, Black Ops: The Life of a CIA Shadow Warrior.
He meets EL PAÍS at the American Museum of the Cuban Diaspora in Miami, and when asked about Cuba, the country he left as a child, he leans forward, aware of the weight of what he is saying. He believes that as soon as the war with Iran ends, the White House will turn its attention back to the Caribbean island, and that the combination of Donald Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, “has given a push” to something that had been stalled for decades.
Prado was born in Cuba in 1950, in Manicaragua, a town at the foot of the Escambray Mountains where Che Guevara established his guerrilla front. He recalls the first gunfight he ever saw as a very small child in the care of a nanny, while he heard “people shooting and falling.” When the Revolution succeeded, the change was “very abrupt,” he says.
His parents learned from a relative that they were on a list to be sent to the Soviet Union. That was when they enrolled him in Operation Peter Pan, the program run by the Catholic Church and the U.S. government that between 1960 and 1962 sent more than 14,000 children alone out of Cuba. Prado arrived in the United States without speaking a word of English and spent several months in an orphanage in Colorado.
As a teenager in South Florida he enlisted in the Air Force, intending to go to Vietnam. He did not arrive in time. By the time he finished his training as a rescue parachutist, the war was ending. He remained in the reserves, worked as a rescuer, and in 1974 handwrote an application to join the CIA. It was rejected.
“They replied with a letter saying they were not looking for people like me,” he recalls. The call came six years later, in 1980, when Ronald Reagan’s Republican administration decided to back the anti-Sandinista guerrillas in Nicaragua and confronted a problem: “The agency did not have a single Hispanic person with the paramilitary credentials I had. They called me and, as the saying goes, the rest is history.”
He spent the following years training the Contras in remote camps on the Honduras–Nicaragua border, and later served in El Salvador, the Philippines and North Korea, always on counterinsurgency and counterterrorism missions. Those years also carried a human cost that rights organizations have documented in detail. Human Rights Watch reported that the Contras carried out kidnappings, torture and systematic executions against the Nicaraguan civilian population in a war that left between 30,000 and 50,000 dead, according to various organizations, throughout the 1980s.
In El Salvador, where Prado arrived at the CIA station in 1986, the civil war’s toll was even greater: about 75,000 civilians died, most at the hands of security forces and death squads, such as those responsible for the El Mozote massacre in 1981, when a battalion trained by the United States killed more than 800 civilians. More than a quarter of El Salvador’s population ended up displaced or exiled, an exodus that became part of communities in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities.

items.title: Cuba in the dark: ‘There are days that go by, the full 24 hours, without electricity’
items.summary: The island, already used to an unstable grid, suffered its seventh total supply collapse this year
items.body_text:
Cuba in the dark: ‘There are days that go by, the full 24 hours, without electricity’
The island, already used to an unstable grid, suffered its seventh total supply collapse this year
In everyday Cubans’ lives there are two unwritten rules. The first is resolver — finding ways to get by. The second is no coger lucha. In other words: keep your composure even when everything is going wrong. But recently both precepts have been pushed to the limit. Squeezed by U.S. sanctions and cornered by decades of mismanagement, islanders have seen that even after hitting rock bottom a new sinkhole always opens. Within hours the country suffered yet another total collapse of the National Electric System (SEN). The second in less than a day, the seventh in 2026, and the eleventh in the past two years.
In Cuba, a country that has learned to live with anomalies better than most, turning on a light bulb has become an act of fiction. The most recent example occurred on Monday. The latest nationwide blackout, which left the island’s nine million residents without power, occurred while operators at the state electric utility were working to restore service after the SEN failure recorded Sunday night. The state company Unión Eléctrica (UNE) confirmed the worst fears when only 14% of Havana — about two million residents — had recovered power. That same weekend the energy system had suffered a partial disconnection that left half the island in the dark.
It’s a story that never ends. Cubans, with their characteristic irony, had long joked that it’s impossible to tell a normal day from one when the SEN collapses. Milagros, 38, a mother of two and a resident of Matanzas in western Cuba, only learned much later that the grid had failed. “The system went out three days ago. That’s what I heard. At the time it went down, we had no power. And without power, we didn’t know if it was real. Cell phones lose service, either coverage or data connection. God forbid an emergency happens and you’re cut off,” she tells EL PAÍS by phone.
SEN collapses
Network collapses should not be confused with power outages. In the first case, the system collapses, so not a single megawatt (MW) is generated across the territory. Outages, on the other hand, occur routinely. They are caused when the country is unable to generate enough electricity to meet demand, or by a localized failure. In recent weeks routine interruptions have exceeded 20 hours in Havana and reached up to 72 consecutive hours in other provinces.
According to the government, the most recent grid collapse was caused by “weather events” that affected the system and “directly impacted the generating units that were online.” For Cuban expert and researcher at the University of Texas’ Institute of the Americas, Jorge Piñón, the latest grid problems “are not only technical failures,” but something more worrying. “[The complications have been in] the transmission lines, which in Cuba are connected to one another like dominoes. If you knock down the first one, they all fall. You can have generation, but if you don’t have the cables to carry that electricity to consumers, it’s useless,” he explains.
Washington’s maximum-pressure campaign, with Cuban-American Senator Marco Rubio as its spearhead, has shaken a system already suffering chronic underfunding. The U.S. squeeze has been delivered in two acts: the capture of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela — Cuba’s main fuel supplier — and the blockage of any tanker attempting to supply Havana under the tariff threat from Donald Trump. Both moves took place earlier this year and have worsened the precarious energy situation even further, not to mention the Republican’s bellicose rhetoric toward the island.

items.title: Bol follows De Bijenkorf in warning of data breach as leaked data appears on dark web
items.summary: Online retailer Bol has warned customers about a data breach involving one of its logistics partners.
items.body_text:
Bol follows De Bijenkorf in warning of data breach as leaked data appears on dark web
Online retailer Bol has warned customers about a data breach involving one of its logistics partners. The company said unauthorized parties accessed the partner's systems, but emphasized that Bol's own systems were not affected. Even so, some customer information may have been viewed or copied, the company said in a statement. Earlier in the day, department store De Bijenkorf also reported a possible data breach. It has since been reported by RTL that the leaked info is currently for sale on the dark web
Like Bol, the incident involved a logistics partner. As a result of the breach at the partner, De Bijenkorf is also experiencing delays in processing customer orders.
Bol said its logistics partner acted immediately after detecting the breach, cutting off unauthorized access and introducing additional security measures. The incident has disrupted part of Bol's logistics network, the company said. Products stored at the affected facility have been temporarily removed from sale, while some customer orders have either been canceled or are expected to arrive later than planned.
Because the incident may have involved the personal data of Bol customers, the company has reported it to the Dutch Data Protection Authority.
Bol told potentially affected customers that the breach occurred at CEVA Logistics, the company responsible for processing and delivering orders from one of its distribution centers.
The retailer warned that attackers may have accessed customer information, including names, addresses, postal codes, places of residence, phone numbers, email addresses, and order details. However, Bol said it has found no evidence so far that payment data, passwords, or account login credentials were exposed.
Bol said it is currently unable to determine how many customers were affected by the incident. The company said the exposed data was limited to information stored in CEVA's affected system for recent orders processed through the impacted distribution center.
The online retailer is advising customers to be extra vigilant for phishing attempts and other forms of fraud. In phishing scams, criminals send fake messages that appear to come from a legitimate organization, often including requests for payment.
Reporting by ANP and NL Times

items.title: Dutch short film Where is my sex drive? wins Student Academy Award
items.summary: The Dutch short film Waar is mijn libido?, released as Where is my sex drive? in English, has won a
items.body_text:
Dutch short film Where is my sex drive? wins Student Academy Award
The Dutch short film Waar is mijn libido?, released as Where is my sex drive? in English, has won a Student Academy Award. Filmmaker Nina Broers won this most important international film prize for students in the Best Alternative or Experimental Film category.
The Student Academy Awards have four categories with three winners per category. In each category, winners receive a gold, silver, or bronze trophy, along with a cash prize of $5,000, $3,000, or $2,000. It is not yet known whether Broers’ film won first, second, or third prize. That will only be announced during the Toronto International Film Festival on September 14.
Broers graduated last year, but made the short film while she was still studying at the St. Joost School of Art & Design in Breda, NOS reports. In the fictional documentary, Broers has two actors reenact scenes from her past. The film also won an award last year at the Go Short Festival, a Dutch film festival for short films.
Broers is the fourth Dutch person to win a Student Academy Award, often referred to as the Oscars for students. Milou Gevers won gold in 2021, Marit Weerheijm won bronze in 2018, and Mike van Diem won in 1990 as the only winner in his category.

items.summary: Trade union CNV has joined FNV in preparing multiple labor actions in September against the government’s plans to cut billions of euros from social security.
items.body_text:
Trade union CNV joins public transport, seaport strikes against social benefits cuts
Trade union CNV has joined FNV in preparing multiple labor actions in September against the government’s plans to cut billions of euros from social security. CNV union members at transport companies in Amsterdam (GVB) and Rotterdam (RET) will receive a call on Thursday to join the nationwide public transport strike on September 9, which FNV announced last week. CNV has already called on port workers to strike on September 4.
“We simply do not accept that the social safety net for the most vulnerable in the Netherlands is being destroyed in such a rigorous manner by this Cabinet. That message must be very clear,” said Tjeerd Orie, action leader at CNV.
FNV had previously announced strikes at port companies in Rotterdam, Amsterdam, and Zeeland, on September 4. The union also announced a nationwide strike in public transport, affecting trains, buses, trams, and metros, on September 9.
With these strikes, the unions demand that the Jetten I Cabinet immediately and entirely scrap the proposed €6.5 billion cut to social security benefits, including state pension (AOW), unemployment (WW), and disability (WIA).
Reporting by ANP and NL Times

items.title: Dutch houseboat owners left high and dry by falling river levels
items.summary: Low water levels in the Rhine delta are causing problems for owners of Dutch houseboats, with no sign of an...
items.body_text:
Dutch houseboat owners left high and dry by falling river levels
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Low water levels in the Rhine delta are causing problems for owners of Dutch houseboats, with no sign of an imminent end to the drought.
Some houseboats and static barges have been standing dry for over a month, resting on platforms that are not designed to support them out of the water or the exposed riverbed.
The Rhine sank to its lowest recorded level last week of 6.46 metres at Lobith, where it enters the Netherlands from Germany, while the flow in the river is one-third of its normal level for July because of low rainfall further upstream.
“We’ve seen these water levels more often in recent years, but usually not until September, and then it gets better after a few days’ rain,” Peter Broekmeulen, board member of the houseboat owners’ association LWO told broadcaster NOS.
The problems for dried-up houseboat owners go further than being stuck above dry land. Several homes have tilted, causing doors and windows to jam and cracks to appear in walls.
Power cables become strained and water pipes crack as they are stretched by the sinking houseboats.
But the biggest challenge is drainage, as residents have had to create improvised systems to deal with waste water that usually flows into the river.
“Open septic tank”
“When the water is there it flows away, but now they’re standing dry it ends up on the land and you get a kind of open septic tank, which is unacceptable from a public health point of view,” Broekmeulen told DutchNews.
Paul van de Veen, who has lived on Rosandepolder in Arnhem, for 40 years, told NOS: “In the early years our boat once had to be towed away by a sailing boat because the water was too high. Now we’re seeing the other side of the coin.”
Van de Veen’s house is still floating after the council dredged his side of the river in February. “We still have a margin,” he said. “The water around us is around a metre deep.”
His neighbours across the water are less fortunate. Marloes Kraal, whose houseboat is in the neighbouring municipality of Renkum, is on a section of river that dried up months ago. “We have cracks in the wall and the roof and there are more appearing,” she said.
The LWO is calling for councils to be more consistent in their policies for houseboats to avoid postcode lotteries arising. Arnhem paid the dredging of the river bank in February from public funds, but in Renkum owners have been told that removing the clay from the riverbed is their own responsibility.
“They are paying the same rent but get much less value for money,” Broekmeulen said. “Legally the council are in the right, but if one council dredges and the other doesn’t, that leads to inequalities.”
Wild west situation
“That’s the wild west situation that we’re up against. We want it to be better regulated nationally for everyone who has to deal with low water levels.”
Owners also face problems when the river levels rise again, as exposed houses can become stuck to their bases, causing them to flood rather than float.
Gert Schols, shipping expert at insurance company EOC, said: “We advise houseboat owners not to go on holiday in periods of extreme drought or arrange a housesitter. You need to keep an eye on what’s happening when the water rises.”
Without action from the government, living on Dutch houseboats risks becoming unappealing in the long term as droughts become more frequent, Broekmeulen warned: “If your house is lying off centre for six months, you’re going to start thinking about moving into one that stands upright.”

items.title: End of a cycling empire? Bike maker Accell at risk of bankruptcy
items.summary: Accell, one of the Netherlands’ biggest bicycle groups, has been granted protection from its creditors to hold off the risk...
items.body_text:
End of a cycling empire? Bike maker Accell at risk of bankruptcy
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Accell, one of the Netherlands’ biggest bicycle groups, has been granted protection from its creditors to hold off the risk of bankruptcy.
The move will give the company court-approved breathing space to try to restructure its debts but leaves its future in doubt.
It is not yet clear how this will impact people with an Accell bike, or for the shops that sell and service them. Neither the company nor the courts have said anything about warranties, spare parts, or outstanding claims from the 2024 recall of tens of thousands of bikes, which were pulled from sale over cracking frames.
Accell owns some of the most well-known names in Dutch cycling – Batavus and Sparta city bikes, Koga touring bikes, and the Babboe and Carqon cargo brands – as well as Raleigh, Lapierre, and the German marques Haibike, Winora, and Ghost. It employs around 3,700 people in 15 countries.
Four difficult years
 The company was publicly listed in Amsterdam until private equity group bought it for €1.56 billion in 2022.
It has struggled ever since the covid pandemic. Demand for bikes surged during the pandemic but parts were hard to get, and by the time supply chains recovered Accell was left with a mountain of unsold stock. Revenues fell 22% in 2024 to just over €1 billion.
A series of cutbacks followed: its warehouse network was reduced from 85 sites to 28, its Turkish factory was sold, and its Heerenveen plant closed last spring, ending its bicycle manufacturing in the Netherlands. Production moved to Hungary and France.
Earlier this year Accell struck a deal with its creditors, who took ownership of the company. That was always a stopgap, and a search for a new owner began. Accell said it held talks with several interested parties, assessed a number of bids, and sought regulatory approval for a possible merger, but no workable solution emerged.

items.body_text:
Double Dutch victory blows Canadian Open tennis draw wide open
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The top two Dutch tennis players, Tallon Griekspoor and Botic van de Zandschulp, have both claimed major scalps in the second round of the Canadian Open.
Griekspoor, who turned 30 last month, put a wretched season behind him to knock out the world number three, top seed and French Open champion Alexander Zverev in three sets.
Zverev appeared to have overcome an early wobble when he rescued a set point before taking the first set on a tie-break.
But Griekspoor hit straight back to take a 4-0 lead in the second set, going on to win 6-2, before breaking the German twice in the decider to win 6-4.
“This is one of my most special wins,” Griekspoor said on court after the match. “There were times this year when I almost threw in the towel.”
Van de Zandschulp matched his achievement as he overcame blustery conditions to see off the Russian number four seed, Daniil Medvedev, in straight sets.
Multiple breaks
In an opening set that featured six breaks of serve, the 30-year-old Dutchman prevailed 6-3. The players broke each other twice in the second before Van de Zandschulp won the tie-break 7-5 with a sublime pass on his second match point.
VAN DE ZANDSCHULP MEDVEDEV! #ZiggoSport #ATP1000 #OBN26 pic.twitter.com/pZauCKqfH8
— Ziggo Sport (@ZiggoSport) August 6, 2026
“It was difficult for me and Daniil to play this evening and I’m happy that I got over the line in the end,” Van de Zandschulp said.
The results leave the draw wide open after world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic opted to sit out the tournament, while the number two player Carlos Alcaraz is recovering from a wrist injury.
Griekspoor will face the Italian Matteo Arnaldi, who knocked him out of this year’s French Open, in the round of 32, while Van de Zandschulp takes on Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz.
Both players are also likely to rise in the ATP rankings from their current positions of 69th for Griekspoor and 70th for Van de Zandschulp as a result of their wins.

items.title: Polish prosecutors end 10-year treason investigation into Tusk over Smolensk air disaster
items.summary: They found that government officials acted in Poland's interests when cooperating with Russia after the crash.
items.body_text:

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński.
The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident.
Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government.
However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place.

Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit.
“They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.”
The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”.
Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash.

The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power.
Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster.
In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run.
However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”.

“We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance.
Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two.
Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News.
Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place.
On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945.
Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski).
Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia.
After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population.

items.title: Estonia and Sweden set rules for holding Swedish prisoners in Tartu
items.summary: A newly signed memorandum lays out everything from clothing and access to television to electricity use and nicotine products, defining how Swedish inmates will live inside Tartu Prison.
items.body_text:
Estonia and Sweden set rules for holding Swedish prisoners in Tartu
A newly signed memorandum lays out everything from clothing and access to television to electricity use and nicotine products, defining how Swedish inmates will live inside Tartu Prison.
The first couple of dozen Swedish prisoners will arrive in Tartu in mid‑August. The exact day will not be disclosed for security reasons, and the public will learn about it only once the prisoners are in their cells. Tartu Prison, which has undergone a refresh renovation, will offer access to Swedish TV channels, but the prisoners will be subject to the Estonian legal system. The rules were clarified in the cooperation memorandum signed on Wednesday.
"We are solving the issue of the Tartu prison standing empty — while being very modern at the same time. Secondly, it is very important for Estonia that we have trained personnel working in the field of internal security. We will train them further at the expense of Swedish taxpayers," said Minister of Justice Liisa Pakosta.
A Swedish prisoner cannot choose whether they serve their sentence in Estonia. But many have shown interest in the possibility.
"My impression is that it is adventurous. It is a historic thing, even for the prisoners," said Niklas Bellström, head of a unit at the Swedish Prison and Probation Service.
In Tartu, prisoners will have access to a gym and can play basketball and football. Swedish prisons generally do not offer such opportunities, but they will have to give up smoking and the popular Swedish snus. As a compromise, the prison's e‑shop will allow weaker nicotine pouches and patches.
"After long and very intense discussions, we finally agreed that nicotine pouches containing synthetic nicotine may be used in the prison. Prisoners will buy them themselves," Pakosta said.
The concession made for Swedes will be extended to Estonian prisoners by end of November at the latest. Cigarettes will remain banned. The biggest concern among Tartu residents is who will come to visit the Swedish prisoners. Each prisoner is guaranteed at least one one‑ to two‑hour visit per month and, once every six months, a longer visit lasting from 24 hours up to three days.
All visits take place on prison grounds, but friends cannot simply show up at the door. Every visitor must apply for permission, and the prison service will check their background. If a visitor may pose a security risk, permission will not be granted.
"In reality, visitors come to about every fifth prisoner, and usually it is a crying mother. We have a very modern prison where inmates have tablets and can hold video meetings," Pakosta said.
Estonia may choose which prisoners it accepts. Terrorists, leaders of organized crime, women and minors will not be taken. No Swedish prisoner will receive city leave, and before release they will be transferred back to Sweden. The average stay in Estonia will be nine months. By the end of the year, there may be 200 Swedish prisoners in Tartu, and next year up to 600.
"Tartu Prison has not caused any concerns for Tartu residents that would undermine their sense of security, and we intend to keep it that way," said Rait Kuuse, head of the prison service.
Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu has promised to terminate the prison‑rental agreement if he comes to power. It cannot be done overnight. Sweden must be notified a year in advance.
"In the event of terminating the agreement, we have 12 months to plan the implementation of that decision," Bellström said.
--
Editor: Johanna Alvin, Argo Ideon

items.title: Eesti 200 head: 67 MPs back Ülle Madise for president
items.summary: Potential presidential candidate Ülle Madise currently has the backing of 67 members of the Riigikogu, Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas said Thursday.
items.body_text:
Eesti 200 head: 67 MPs back Ülle Madise for president
Potential presidential candidate Ülle Madise currently has the backing of 67 members of the Riigikogu, Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas said Thursday.
"Our three parties together account for 63 votes, because Zuzu Izmailova has said she will not support her, and as far as I know there are three independent MPs. That makes 67 votes," Kallas said when asked how much support Madise currently has.
A presidential candidate needs at least 68 votes to be elected in the Riigikogu.
Madise has been endorsed by the governing Reform Party, which has 37 MPs, along with two independent lawmakers. Eesti 200 has 13 MPs, while the opposition Social Democratic Party (SDE) has nine MPs, with five additional lawmakers voting alongside the party. One of those five, Izmailova, has said she will not support Madise. Based on those figures, the three parties together would have 65 votes, meaning they would still need at least three votes from independent MPs to elect the president.
Asked about the remaining shortfall, Kallas replied: "What's missing is support from Isamaa or the Center Party."
"Ülle Madise has the broadest support in the Riigikogu today, but the final outcome — whether Ülle Madise becomes the next president — now depends on the decisions of the Center Party and Isamaa," she added.
"Why they are not telling the people of Estonia what that decision is, I don't understand. I believe the statesmanlike thing to do would be to say clearly that if Ülle Madise is nominated — and there is no problem in submitting the required 21 signatures as early as tomorrow, even though the deadline is still some time away — then would Isamaa and would the Center Party support Ülle Madise? That answer is the missing piece in knowing whether Ülle Madise will become the next president," said Education and Research Minister Kallas.
She added that she sees no reason why any party should refuse to support Madise.
"I don't see any reason, except for partisan interests ahead of the parliamentary elections — wishing to paint the government as incapable and to derail the presidential election for that purpose. Not because Ülle Madise would be unsuitable as president. Ülle Madise enjoys very strong public support in Estonia, but unfortunately, in some cases partisan interests outweigh the interests of society," she said.
According to Kallas, Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise is a highly capable, competent and widely respected public figure who is well suited to serve as president.
The Riigikogu will convene to elect the president on September 2, 2026. A presidential candidate must be nominated by at least one-fifth of the Riigikogu's members (21 MPs). Candidates must be Estonian citizens by birth who are at least 40 years old. Active-duty members of the armed forces and anyone who has already served two consecutive terms as president are ineligible. If no candidate is elected in the Riigikogu, the election will be decided by the Electoral College where MPs are joined by local government electors.
Key dates:
August 21–24: Nomination period for candidates.
September 2: First round of voting in the Riigikogu.
September 3: Second and third rounds of voting in the Riigikogu, if necessary.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mait Ots

items.title: Tallinn will not rebuild drainage system for cleaner Inglirand water
items.summary: Tallinn does not plan to rebuild the stormwater drainage system to clean the water at Inglirand beach. Instead, it is trying to identify illegal wastewater connections, Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan said.
items.body_text:
Tallinn will not rebuild drainage system for cleaner Inglirand water
Tallinn does not plan to rebuild the stormwater drainage system to clean the water at Inglirand beach. Instead, it is trying to identify illegal wastewater connections, Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan said.
For years, one of Tallinn's most prominent waterfront areas has been known for its unpleasant odor and polluted water.
"Naturally, we want our beaches and coastal waters to be in good condition and pleasant and safe for both residents and the ecosystem," Järvan told ERR.
"The main cause of the unpleasant smell along the shores of Tallinn Bay is algae, whose growth is fueled by the water's high nutrient content," the deputy mayor said.
"Looking at the broader picture, the vast majority of the nutrient load in Tallinn Bay comes from the Pirita River, with the sources located mainly within the river's watershed. Agriculture is responsible for the largest share of that pollution and there are no quick or easy solutions to reduce its impact," Järvan said.
In 2021, the then-head of Tallinn's Kesklinn district said he hoped Inglirand would become an official public swimming beach. The beach was revitalized following the completion of Reidi tee, when the shoreline was also renovated. However, the Health Board has repeatedly warned that swimming in the waters at Inglirand may be unsafe.
Last summer, then-Kesklinn district head Sander Andla (Reform) said the root of the problem was that several stormwater outfalls, as well as a port, are located near Inglirand.
At the time, Andla said the only solution would be to relocate the stormwater outfalls farther away. "As for the timeline, it's important to understand that this isn't the kind of job that can be completed in a week by three people. It would cost the city several million euros," Andla said.
According to Järvan, redirecting the stormwater flowing into the Inglirand area is not a realistic solution because it would require extensive reconstruction of the stormwater drainage systems in Kesklinn and Lasnamäe. "That is why the city is focusing on improving stormwater quality, including identifying illegal wastewater connections to the stormwater drainage system," Järvan said.
"To that end, the city has commissioned a study to identify possible sources of pollution. Because the watershed being examined is large, the first study was unable to identify them. The search for pollution sources will continue and additional studies will be commissioned if necessary," Järvan added.
--
Editor: Aleksander Krjukov, Marcus Turovski

Party of Freedom and Justice (SSP) leader Dragan Djilas said on Thursday that Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has proclaimed himself the âgreatest ruler in Serbian history,â while in reality leaving the country âmore indebted and isolated than ever.â

In a press release, Djilas argued that Vucic is spreading lies by claiming Serbia is currently âat its strongest in history â economically, politically, and militarily.â He added that a greater concern is the presidentâs attempt to frame his time in power as the most successful era the country has ever seen.
Djilas pointed out that Vucicâs claims of being âmore successful than Emperor Dusan, Stefan the Tallâ and all others who âbuilt and defended the Serbian state over the centuriesâ are a âdangerous manifestation of a cult of personality.â He described the president as a man who has âlost all touch with reality and is convinced that history begins and ends with him.â
According to Djilas, the true legacy of Vucicâs rule includes ârecord-breaking debt, captured institutions, a degraded education system, and the ruin of the agricultural and energy sectors.â He added that the country has become a âchampion of corruptionâ and sits at the very back of the line in the EU accession process.
The SSP leader also dismissed the claim of Serbiaâs record strength as factually incorrect, noting that the public debt has surpassed 41 billion euro, the domestic economy is facing severe crises, and the Serbian Armed Forces are suffering from a manpower shortage.

items.title: ‘Our Parents Carried us to Safety’: Disabled Kosovo Children Recall Escape in 1999
items.summary: In March 1999, as Serbian forces expelled Kosovo Albanian families from their homes, Sali Morina and his wife had to carry three of their children, all suffering from muscular dystrophy, by hand to safety.
items.body_text:
"In late March, Serbian forces were surrounding the villages," Sali Morina recalls of Kosovo in 1999. "I carried both our sons and my mother to the car, while my wife carried Ganimete [their daughter] because she was easier to carry."
The Morina family, from the village of Samadrexha, in the southern municipality of Suhareke/Suva Reka, were among the hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians expelled during the war in 1998-99 as Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic stepped up his campaign against the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA.
The Morinas found flight harder than many: three of their five children have muscular dystrophy, a condition that causes progressive muscle weakness and loss of muscle mass. They had no wheelchairs to ease their escape.
Nearly three decades later, their story is one of those told in the “Exodus 99” exhibition at BIRN’s Reporting House station in the Kosovo capital of Pristina.
Housed in a restored railway wagon at Pristina train station – the same place where thousands of Kosovo Albanians were forced onto overcrowded trains during the war – the exhibition documents the experiences of civilians violently expelled by Serbian forces in 1999.
As NATO started to bomb Yugoslavia to force Serbian forces out of Kosovo, nearly one million Kosovo Albanians fled, forced onto roads leading to Albania and what is now North Macedonia.
The Morina family left by car while one of their teenage sons drove the family tractor with some of their belongings. Serbian forces stopped them in the village of Bellanic, before they were able to join a mass convoy heading for Albania.
Ganimete Morina, who was nine at the time, remembers the uniforms of the Serbian police and military. “They were wearing masks, hats and camouflage nets,” she recalls.
“Three or four policemen approached our car. They knocked on the window and ordered my father to hand over the car. They pointed a rifle at his ear and said: ‘Will you take the children out, or should we kill you in front of them?’”
Visitors look at the restored railway wagon at Pristina train station. Photo: BIRN
Her father recalls: “They took my car because they liked it. It was a [Volkswagen] Golf Mk2,” he says. His disabled children were “left in the mud” by the side of the road, he adds.
“We had no wheelchairs,” Ganimete notes. “My mother and father carried us everywhere.”
One by one, Sali carried each of the children onto a village bus that was already crowded with other displaced Kosovo Albanians. “We spent the whole night in there,” he recalls.
“There must have been more than 100 people in that bus,” says Ganimete. “My father held my two brothers on his lap, and my mother held me.”
As the bus waited to leave, she watched Serbian forces separate young men from the crowd. “They took them to a garage and beat them. We could see it from the bus.”
She also remembers police demanding money and gold jewelry from refugees.
After spending the night on the bus, they were ordered to head towards Malisheva the next morning.
“When we arrived, Serbian police and paramilitaries had set up a checkpoint. I saw people being killed there. I thought: ‘This is where our lives will end,’” says Sali.
As they travelled through Kosovo, scenes of destruction unfolded around them. “We saw houses burning the entire way. We saw bodies lying by the roadside,” he adds.
A shocking memory that has stayed with him is of a young man trapped beneath his overturned tractor trailer in Rahovec: “I could hear him screaming, but nobody could help him. Today, there is a memorial to him there.”
At the border with Albania, the Serbian police became suspicious of one of Morina’s sons.
“They told me: ‘This one is wounded. Where are you taking him? He’s a KLA soldier.’ I explained that he had a disability and couldn’t walk. I pulled up his legs so they could see,, he says.
That moment remains among Ganimete’s worst memories: “I’ll never forget how my father lifted my brother to show his legs. The policeman narrowed his eyes

items.title: Serbia’s Vucic Accused of “Vote-Buying” With Cash Pledges
items.summary: Experts fear the newly-announced payments for all adult citizens in Serbia, announced by Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic, are part of a political campaign rather than a social measure.
items.body_text:
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has announced a set of financial payments for all adult citizens in Serbia, alongside subsidies for various groups – leaving critics wondering whether the measures are an attempt at vote-buying.
In early July, Vucic announced during an appearance on RTS that the state would likely provide financial assistance to all citizens aged 18 or older, emphasising that the funds would not come from the state budget. Two weeks later Vucic gave more detail during a Morning programme on TV Prva, announcing two payments for adults scheduled for September.
“Payments will be made to pensioners and to those entitled to benefits under the pensioners’ welfare system. Separate payments will be made to those receiving social benefits. On top of all that, we are also proceeding with this payment from the Share Fund for all adult citizens, which we would not be able to do without adding around 150 million euros from the budget,” Vucic said.

items.title: IVF for Single Women Raises New Conflict of Interest Questions for Czech PM
items.summary: The Czech government is planning to give single women access to assisted reproduction services. Might the PM’s own stake in the fertility market have something to do with it?
items.body_text:
Even ethics experts are divided on the issue.
Czech Health Minister Adam Vojtech turned to his ministry’s ethics committee for counsel at the end of July to ascertain its views on whether Czechia should legalise IVF and assisted reproduction techniques for single women. But the 23-member advisory board could not reach agreement, delaying their final assessment until they reconvene after the summer.
Supporters of the reform argue that a woman’s relationship status should not be a defining factor excluding them from motherhood. Opponents, on the other hand, say assisted reproduction is first and foremost a treatment for infertility problems in couples, not a reproductive health service that should be available to anyone.
Few topics carry as much biological, ethical, sociological and political weight, and the debate is bound to intensify after the government and parliament return to work after the summer recess.
Bringing IVF to single women
The ethics committee’s inconclusive discussions did not prevent Health Minister Vojtech – a member of the ruling ANO party and close ally of Prime Minister Andrej Babis – from continuing to push his draft bill and taking it to the next step for discussion.
Compared with most of Europe, Czechia’s reproductive policies remain relatively strict to this day. It is also one of the few EU member states where women without a male partner cannot access artificial insemination techniques – along with the likes of Slovakia, Poland, Lithuania and Italy – thus making them only available, on paper, to heterosexual couples.
“There is a large group of single women who are secure and would like to have a child, but they cannot legally have one in the Czech Republic,” said Nicole Mardesicova, vice-chairwoman of the assisted reproduction department at the Czech Gynaecological and Obstetrics Society.
The draft amendment, submitted on June 24 for interdepartmental consultation by Health Minister Vojtech together with the government’s human rights commissioner, Tatana Mala, would update the Act on Special Health Services, which many have long criticised as outdated. It states, for example, that “artificial insemination may be performed on a woman of childbearing age… upon a written request from the woman and man who intend to undergo this heath service together.”
In its current form, the reform would merely abolish the requirement for a man’s written permission, opening up assisted reproduction to single women and, implicitly, to lesbian couples.
It would, however, keep other regulations in their current format: only women up to 49 years old can access those services, and public health insurance only covers their reimbursement for women under 40 and for a limited number of attempts.
Based on the Health Ministry’s proposal, women making the request alone would, however, not be covered by health insurance and should cover the costs on a self-pay basis regardless of age or number of attempts. This, in turn, raises another question on whether the access will be de-facto reserved for wealthier women who can afford it.
“There are women who, for various reasons, do not have a partner. What is important to me is that they are here, they are interested, and I do not think that the state should prevent them from having a child if they are able to take care of it,” reasoned Vojtech.
“Moreover, the need to have a partner is already being circumvented: they can come with any acquaintance or friend who declares themselves as their partner, and the centre providing artificial insemination has no way of verifying this,” he added.
Political clash
The proposal has been welcomed by associations and activists who have long pushed, behind the scenes, for the liberalisation of reproductive rights, and is seen as a key step in the right direction for those seeing the exclusion of single women as a shameful injustice.
But even within the government itself, Vojtech’s plans are setting up a political clash with ANO’s two coalition partners

items.title: Monetary Council Says Further Base Rate Cuts Remain Possible
items.summary: Mihály Varga, Governor of the Hungarian Central Bank (MNB) At their meeting on July 21, the members of the Monetary Council of the Hungarian Central Bank (MNB) voted unanimously to lower the key interest rate. The Council lowered the central bank’s key interest rate by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent, with both limits of […] The post Monetary Council Says Further Base Rate Cuts Remain Possible appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
Speaking at a meeting of central bank governors in Baku, Mihály Varga stressed the importance of price stability, financial resilience, and digital innovation.Continue reading
At their meeting on July 21, the members of the Monetary Council of the Hungarian Central Bank (MNB) voted unanimously to lower the key interest rate.
The Council lowered the central bank’s key interest rate by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent, with both limits of the interest rate corridor also being reduced by 25 basis points each.
The policymakers agreed that, should favorable developments continue, there was room for further cuts to the key interest rate over the course of the summer while ensuring positive real interest rates; the Council will decide on the continuation of this policy in September based on the inflation report.
The Council noted that the lower risk premium for domestic assets persists.
Policy makers emphasized that, although the forint had depreciated in tandem with the rise in energy prices, domestic financial markets remained relatively stable.
With regard to inflation trends and the inflation outlook, Council members noted that these had developed more favorably than projected in June. Based on the documents, some policymakers pointed out that the pace of price increases remained below the lower bound of the tolerance range, while others emphasized that inflation was below the central bank’s June forecast. Several members highlighted that public inflation expectations have moderated since the beginning of the year.
There was consensus within the Council that the inflation outlook and the persistently low risk premium for domestic investments have preserved the scope for monetary policy action. In addition, some Council members pointed out that the domestic real interest rate remains relatively high compared with those in other emerging markets. Against this backdrop, policymakers saw an opportunity to continue the series of three interest rate cuts announced in June. Several Council members emphasized that this step was consistent with the foreseeable monetary policy course.
In its July interest rate decision, the Monetary Council discussed a single proposed resolution: to lower the key interest rate by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent.
According to the minutes, Council members continuously assess the inflation outlook, global developments, and trends in the domestic risk premium.
Via MTI; Featured photo: MTI/Kovács Márton

items.title: Intimidation and Revenge – If Grandchildren Ever Ask How This Was Possible in Hungary Back Then
items.summary: Hungary is, de facto, once again a one-party state: thunderous applause, just like in the days of Stalinism “Because back then they were like you are today!” – Henryk M. Broder’s striking answer to the question of how the Nazi Party (NSDAP) was able to rise to power in the 1930s also lends itself as […] The post Intimidation and Revenge – If Grandchildren Ever Ask How This Was Possible in Hungary Back Then appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
The “Pedo-Fidesz” label attached to Viktor Orbán’s party served the same purpose: to discredit a political rival.Continue reading
“Because back then they were like you are today!” – Henryk M. Broder’s striking answer to the question of how the Nazi Party (NSDAP) was able to rise to power in the 1930s also lends itself as an explanation for present-day Hungary.
Since Hungary’s Soviet Republic and the terror of the Arrow Cross regime were both relatively short-lived, they could easily be dismissed as unfortunate aberrations in an otherwise coherent national history. The much longer period of arbitrary rule under communist ideology, meanwhile, was conveniently explained away through the Yalta narrative. Yet the seamless transition of many Hungarians from serving the brown henchmen to the red ones is by no means a uniquely Hungarian phenomenon.
Turncoats may well constitute, in every nation, the critical mass indispensable for every major political shift.
In Hungary, however, the more troubling question is how the current system of arbitrary rule came to power. “Because today you are what they once were.” A cliché, perhaps—but one that bears repeating, especially since the ideology of progress continues to be invoked as the principal framework for interpreting human nature.
Anyone wishing to understand the mindset of Zoltán Tarr or Bálint Ruff would do well to take a glance at history, even if the frailty of human nature (natura lapsa) remains the enduring explanation that transcends historical eras. One need not be a psychologist to recognize the psychological forces driving the revolutionary zeal of these two men.
Ruff, the Minister heading the Prime Minister’s Office, is the archetypal apparatchik, unwaveringly consistent with himself. Tarr, the Minister of Culture, is the ideologically fluid careerist.
The former remained loyal to his internationalist worldview even during what the author calls the “16 years in the wilderness.” His colleague, by contrast—like Stalin, who initially intended to serve God—ultimately succumbed to the temptation of power, deciding that climbing the career ladder mattered more than ascending Jacob’s ladder.
Tarr is a master of grandstanding. Fortunately, he never served as an active pastor, for serving others is clearly not his calling. He is the quintessential ecclesiastical careerist—someone for whom the Reformed Church could no longer provide the opportunities for further advancement that he sought. During the election campaign, he remained deliberately vague (“First we have to win the election; after that, anything is possible”), but once the new government took office, he quickly became one of its most outspoken members.
Although he is formally responsible for culture and social affairs, he could just as easily head a cross-ministerial portfolio for intimidation and coercion.
Substantive policymaking is virtually absent from his ministry. Instead, it is characterized by investigations, settling scores, and lengthy tirades against the work of his predecessors—activities that seem to give him obvious satisfaction while causing growing concern among his often unwilling audiences. Anyone who still remembers communist officials and the way they treated the working population can hardly escape the impression that the same destructive spirit is at work once again. Younger generations, meanwhile, may be reminded of Marvel’s Ghost Rider: like the “Spirit of Vengeance,” Tarr appears determined to make alleged sinners suffer for the pain they have—at least in his own perception—inflicted on others.
Ruff, for all his narrow-mindedness, is the idealistic man of the Left—fiat iustitia et pereat mundus (“Let justice be done, though the world perish”). items.title: The Timeline of a Public Broadcast Appointment in the New Hungarian Dictatorship
items.summary: Péter Magyar’s Facebook governance claims another victim. As we have reported earlier this week, it took a single casual Facebook comment from Hungary’s increasingly volatile Prime Minister to remove the newly appointed Editor-in-chief of the public broadcaster’s M1 news channel. In a timeline of the events published yesterday, Gábor Hajdú gives his personal account […] The post The Timeline of a Public Broadcast Appointment in the New Hungarian Dictatorship appeared first on Hungary Today.
items.body_text:
"I do not think so", said Magyar on Facebook, triggering a panicked response from managers.Continue reading
As we have reported earlier this week, it took a single casual Facebook comment from Hungary’s increasingly volatile Prime Minister to remove the newly appointed Editor-in-chief of the public broadcaster’s M1 news channel. In a timeline of the events published yesterday, Gábor Hajdú gives his personal account of that Orwellian day early this August.
“In response to the events of the past few days, as one of the key figures in this case, I feel it is necessary to set the record straight, even though the truth only serves to confuse many people—including several opinion leaders who have reported on the matter.
First of all, I would like to state that the new leadership of public media has placed me and my family in an extremely undignified and humiliating situation, because they removed me from my position within 24 hours using the very same justification they had used to invite me to take on this honorable role.”
Namely, in both cases, they cited the need to restore the credibility of public media.”
“I left public media in 2015, after M1 became a news channel, to join Hír TV, which, starting in February of that same year ceased to be “Fidesz-aligned.” As the editor-in-chief of news programs, I strove—together with my colleagues—to achieve balance. In 2018, I did indeed move to Echo Television. After the then-management of Hír TV committed itself to Jobbik—a move I believed violated the principle of balance—I did not want to be a part of it. At Echo TV, as an editor-in-charge, I also produced news programs in accordance with the same principles, working alongside excellent colleagues who adhered to journalistic standards. Although I had not physically moved—sitting at the same desk, in the same chair—I effectively returned to Hír TV”
…Reality has slammed the door in our faces far more brutally than any prediction could have foreseen, and we are facing one of its grave consequences these days.
Instead of a sober discussion of these issues—or even the desirable role of public television—news of an appointment has devolved into a virtual lynching… Although most people are now questioning Balázs Bodacz’s (public broadcaster news director, ed. note) responsibility, it is worth noting that the entire management was fully aware of my professional background, and the CEO signed my employment contract with that knowledge. Just as space has its geometry and a place has its spirit, so too do numbers have their value and words their weight. The coordinate system for those particular 24 hours is as follows:
9:00 a.m. Signing of the employment contract at the TV headquarters on Kunigunda Way.
9:30 a.m. Meeting with the news director
10:00 a.m. Visit to the newsroom; greetings with colleagues I have not seen in a long time and new colleagues
10:30 a.m. Studio tour
11:30 a.m. Moving into the office
12:00 p.m. Branding meeting
1:30 p.m. Lunch with a former colleague
2:00 p.m. Administrative tasks, handling phone calls
5:00 p.m. Leaving the headquarters
7:42 p.m. MTI (Hungarian News Agency, ed. note) publishes the news about the appointment, which is picked up by news portals. Following this, the prime minister (Péter Magyar, ed. note) adds a comment to the news item appearing on Telex, which reads:
“I don’t think so…”
At 9:24 p.m., I receive a call informing me that I have become a burden that public media cannot bear
2:00 p.m. Signing of the termination of the employment contract
After I accepted the job offered by the management of public television—quitting my previous job to do so—they fired me without cause, taking advantage of the legal provision regarding the probationary period. I surely do not need to explain that it was not because I did something wrong on that one particular day.
If I was a propagandist because of Hír TV, then are not those who worked there at the same time as me also propagandists who no longer have a place in

items.title: Hétfő reggelig lehet köztársasági elnököt jelölni
items.summary: Hivatalosan is kitűzte az államfőválasztást az Országgyűlés alelnöke. A Tisza frakciója szombaton dönt a jelöltjéről.
items.body_text:
Hétfő reggelig lehet köztársasági elnököt jelölni
Hivatalosan is kitűzte az államfőválasztást Hallerné Nagy Anikó, az Országgyűlés alelnöke. A titkos szavazást a Tisza-frakció kezdeményezésére jövő kedden tartják.
A parlament oldalán megosztott dokumentumból az is kiderült, hogy hétfő reggel 10 óra a jelölés határideje. Ahhoz, hogy valakinek a neve felkerüljön a szavazólapra, az országgyűlési képviselők legalább egyötödének, azaz 40 képviselőnek az ajánlására van szükség. Minden képviselő csak egy jelöltet ajánlhat, és ha valaki ezt nem tartja be, akkor mindegyik ajánlása érvénytelen lesz. Az ajánlásokat a házbizottság hétfőn 12:30-kor kezdődő ülésén tekintik át.
A Tisza Párt még nem jelentette be, hogy kit jelölnek a posztra. Erről a párt közleménye szerint szombaton döntenek. Bujdosó Andrea, a párt frakcióvezetője az MTI-nek azt mondta: a jelöltek kiválasztása még folyamatban van, de a céljuk az, hogy a szombati frakcióülésen több ember közül válasszanak. Neveket nem árult el, de közölte, hogy még egyeztetnek arról, hogyan mutatják be államfőjelöltjüket.
Magyar Péter korábban azt kérte a magyaroktól, hogy ajánljanak neveket az államfői posztra, majd alig egy nappal ezután már be is jelentette, hogy szerinte a sakkozó Polgár Judit lenne a legalkalmasabb a feladatra. Sokan vitatták ezt az eljárást és Polgár személyét is, aki végül visszautasította a felkérést. Magyar később Romsics Ignác Széchenyi-díjas történésszel, a Vidéki prókátor néven ismertté vált ügyvéddel, Fülöp Botonddal, majd szerdán Baka Andrással, a Legfelsőbb Bíróság korábbi elnökével találkozott, de az nem derült ki, hogy ezeken a megbeszéléseken szóba került-e az esetleges jelölésük. Kerestük emiatt az érintetteket, de nem reagáltak. Nem kizárt, hogy közülük kerül ki a Tisza Párt jelöltje.
Rajtuk kívül egyedül a 44 fős Fidesz-frakció tudna önállóan köztársasági elnököt állítani, a KDNP vagy a Mi Hazánk a Fidesz nélkül nem tudja ezt megtenni. A Fidesz és a KDNP azonban korábban azt jelezte, hogy bojkottálják az államfőválasztást, mert illegitimnek tartják Sulyok Tamás eltávolítását. A Mi Hazánk múlt héten Tóth Máté energiajogászt jelölte a posztra, ami más frakciók támogatása nélkül tulajdonképpen csak szimbolikus gesztusnak tekinthető.
A köztársasági elnököt az országgyűlési képviselők kétharmada választja meg titkos szavazással, és a szavazás eredményének kihirdetését követő nyolcadik napon, azaz augusztus 19-én léphet hivatalba. Megbízatása az Alaptörvény 17. módosítása értelmében az új Alkotmány hatálybalépéséig, de legfeljebb öt évre szól majd.
