items.title: Why applicants with top scores still get rejected by US universities
items.summary: Admissions officers at universities in the U.S. choose students that fit into a class rather than those with excellent academic results, officials from the University of Michigan and Dartmouth College said at a seminar in Vietnam.
items.body_text:
Erica Sanders, assistant vice provost and executive director of undergraduate admissions at Michigan, said the school adopted a test-optional policy in 2024 and remains test optional for the current cycle.
Scores are not what decides an application, Sanders said.
Christina Moreland, associate director of admissions at Dartmouth, said the college still runs a holistic review, a practice it has used since 1921.
Dartmouth reinstated its SAT and ACT requirement in 2024, joining Yale, Brown, MIT and Georgetown, with Princeton following for fall 2027 entry.
Officers work through a set of questions on each applicant. The first is whether the student can handle the academic pressure.
Others cover what they have done with the opportunities available to them, what they care about, and what they would bring to the campus.
Admissions staff at both schools still read every application individually, Sanders said, despite the spread of artificial intelligence through teaching and learning.
At the final stage, officers pick students who fit together into a class that matches each school's priorities. Thus, applicants with very high scores would be turned away while others with thinner records but a distinctive profile get in.
Students should not chase a template that is not who they are, or take on activities purely to fill an application, or assume a research project is needed to convince a committee, the two said at the seminar on U.S. higher education trends held by IIG Vietnam and the College Board last month.
They also warned against rushing the essay or using it to list achievements.
Sanders said U.S. universities are recruiting harder abroad as the domestic pool shrinks.
Research by the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education, funded in part by the College Board, projects that U.S. high school graduates peaked in 2025 at 3.9 million and will fall to 3.4 million by 2041, a drop of 13%.
Sanders said applicants should weigh five factors when choosing among the more than 4,000 U.S. universities she counted.
The first is whether to go public or private. Public universities tend to be large with broad academic offerings, while private schools are smaller and more specialized.
The second is the route in. Rather than entering a four-year university directly, international students can start at a community college and transfer, which gives them time to adjust to the language and the classroom.
The rest are location and the community around the campus, the cost and what scholarships are available, and what the school offers outside the classroom.
U.S. institutions hosted 1,177,766 international students in the 2024-2025 academic year, according to the Institute of International Education's Open Doors report.
Vietnam sent 25,584 of them, up from 22,066, becoming the fifth-largest source country after India, China, South Korea and Canada.
Michigan ranks third among U.S. public universities and 20th overall in the 2026 U.S. News & World Report rankings, with 34,454 undergraduates. It hosted 11,929 international students in 2024-2025, more than all but 10 U.S. institutions.
Dartmouth, a member of the Ivy League, enrolls about 6,900 students, including 4,637 undergraduates.

items.title: Vietnamese students denied Taiwan visas as graduation paperwork rules change
items.summary: Vietnamese students bound for Taiwan risk missing their enrollment dates after Taipei's representative offices began requiring full high school diplomas for student visas.
items.body_text:
Several parents in Ho Chi Minh City told VnExpress their children had been refused visas despite holding admission letters and enrollment notices from Taiwanese universities.
The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City said in a recent notice that from the 2026 academic year it will accept applications only from candidates holding an official diploma.
It cited instructions from Taiwan's foreign affairs authority and its own education division, and Vietnam's decision to stop issuing the provisional graduation certificate applicants previously used while waiting for their diplomas.
Applicants could previously submit either an official diploma or the provisional certificate.
Vietnam's Ministry of Education and Training made that change in Circular 13/2026, signed March 9 and effective April 24. It merged the provisional certificate and the separate exam results certificate into one document, the certificate of exam results, issued by the school where the student sat the exam.
Schools must now issue the diploma within 30 days of the student receiving that certificate.
"They have less than a month before they need to be there to enroll. I hope all sides resolve this soon, because it is not the students' fault," one parent said.
Lam Vi Chi, head of the education division and education counselor at TECO in Ho Chi Minh City, confirmed to VnExpress that many Vietnamese students were struggling with the visa process, without giving a figure.
Visa policy falls to Taiwan's foreign affairs authority, which set the requirement and then informed the education authority, he said. If Vietnamese schools are still issuing provisional certificates, he added, the education ministry would need to tell both TECO offices in writing.
He said some universities in Taiwan would discuss with the education ministry regarding the matter, helping students to get admitted.
An official at the Ho Chi Minh City education department said it had sped up its process and issued diplomas early to about 280 students bound for Taiwan. Others are due to receive theirs from next week.
Taiwanese universities generally start on Sept. 7, though some ask students to arrive between Aug. 29 and 31 for registration, health checks, orientation and residency paperwork.
Taiwanese rules let a student enroll for a term if they arrive before a third of the semester has passed, but universities set their own deadlines.
Taiwan's education authority recorded 52,974 Vietnamese students at its colleges and universities in 2025, up 13,364 from 2024 and past 50,000 for the first time, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.
Vietnam has been Taiwan's largest source of international students for several years and supplies roughly 30% of the total.

items.title: Thailand to adopt checked baggage opening without owners present
items.summary: Authorities in Thailand will be able to open air travellers’ checked baggage for security reasons without an owner’s consent starting on Oct 16, but the Civil Aviation Authority of Thailand (CAAT) has affirmed that checks will follow strict guidelines.
items.body_text:
Authorities in Thailand will be able to open air travellers’ checked baggage for security reasons without an owner’s consent starting on Oct 16, but the Civil Aviation Authority of Thailand (CAAT) has affirmed that checks will follow strict guidelines.
According to the CAAT, officials will open only checked bags bound for an aircraft’s hold that have been x-rayed and suspected to contain illegal objects or items that could jeopardise aircraft safety.
Suspicious bags will be opened in specified areas. The opening will be videoed and evidence will be collected throughout the process so that the action can be checked. Luggage owners will be informed of the opening afterwards.
The CAAT recommended that travellers use luggage with an approved TSA Lock system, which will allow security officers to open luggage without damaging it.
The regulator said the practice was now standard in countries including Singapore, Japan, South Korea, the United States and many countries in Europe and the Middle East. It also helps prevent travel delays because officials do not have to call luggage owners before the opening, the CAAT said.
The new measure was first announced in February to give the parties concerned time to prepare, and for passengers to review the status of their luggage if necessary.
Once the inspection system takes effect, travellers with concerns can file complaints at the CAAT complaint portal.

items.title: Body of popular Thai YouTuber Hlun Solo returns home
items.summary: The body of the popular Thai travel YouTuber Hlun Solo was returned to Thailand early Thursday morning, as his family prepared to seek an autopsy to find the cause of his death in Georgia last month.
items.body_text:
The body of the popular Thai travel YouTuber Hlun Solo was returned to Thailand early Thursday morning, as his family prepared to seek an autopsy to find the cause of his death in Georgia last month.
The body was transported on a Turkish Airlines flight from Istanbul that landed at Suvarnabhumi airport at 5.10am.
After the autopsy is completed in Bangkok, the family intends to bring the body to Somdet district of Kalasin for funeral rites, said Jaithai Upakarnitikaset, spokeswoman for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Bowornthat Pengsuk, better known as Hlun Solo, died in Tbilisi, Georgia, on July 14. Police there confirmed the death on July 29, two days after the family issued a public appeal for news about the 27-year-old’s whereabouts.
The family said they had not heard from Bowornthat since July 13, shortly after he arrived in the Caucasus nation to gather material for one of his popular features on solo budget travel.
Police in Georgia said his body was found at a hotel room in the capital city, with circumstances surrounding the death described as unclear.
The Thai embassy in Ankara, Turkey, which also handles Thai affairs in Georgia, sent officials to Tbilisi to coordinate the return of Hlun Solo’s remains.
Hlun Solo had 2.5 million followers on Facebook and 950,000 subscribers to his YouTube channel at the time of his death, and as of Thursday those figures had grown to 3.9 million and 1.3 million, respectively.

items.title: Rising yen set to boost Japanese tourism
items.summary: A stronger yen as a result of US-Japan currency interventions could incentivise more Japanese to travel overseas, especially to short-haul destinations such as Thailand, while Thai travellers should not be discouraged from visiting Japan, according to tourism operators.
items.body_text:
A stronger yen as a result of US-Japan currency interventions could incentivise more Japanese to travel overseas, especially to short-haul destinations such as Thailand, while Thai travellers should not be discouraged from visiting Japan, according to tourism operators.
Yoshida Masahiro, a committee member of the Association of Thai Travel Agents, said a sharp rise in the yen could persuade more Japanese tourists to travel overseas as a result of cheaper tour packages.
The Japanese currency has rebounded from 40-year lows near 164 to the US dollar to reach a range of 155-157, as America is collaborating with Tokyo to intervene in the yen as the nation struggles with high import costs and mounting public debt.
According to Mr Yoshida, Japan tourism operators are promoting two-way travel, encouraging them to travel abroad after Japan recorded the highest number of international arrivals last year, partly due to a weak yen.
Over the past few years, a weak yen prompted Japanese tourists to scale down their trips, such as cutting their stays from five- to four-star hotels, he noted.
"The impact of a stronger yen may become clearer as early as next year, since many tourists have already booked and paid their travel packages for the upcoming months, and the currency just entered the early ramp-up period," said Mr Yoshida.
Other factors are encouraging the Japanese to travel overseas, such as the Nikkei closing at an all-time-high in June, lifting the spending of many Japanese companies organising overseas meetings and group incentives for their employees.
"Thailand should reap benefits from this trend as the country remains a popular destination for short-haul travelling from Japan, especially during summer like this month, while long-haul trips are being pressured by high airfares and the prolonged Middle East crisis," Mr Yoshida said.
The Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) expects 1.1 million Japanese arrivals this year, relatively unchanged from 1.09 million reported last year, partly due to the war in the Middle East.
Pattaranong Na Chiangmai, deputy governor for Asia and South Pacific Markets at TAT, said the agency may increase the projection later this year if the Japanese economy improves and the yen continues to appreciate.
This could encourage more Japanese to spend money and travel abroad, including to Thailand, she said.
Kanlayanee Assanee, president of the Thai Travel Agents Association, said the rebounding yen should not significantly impact Thai tourists in the short term since travellers have already booked their trips ahead of time.
Mrs Kanlayanee said Japan remains among the top outbound destinations for Thai tourists, due to its infrastructure, safety, and its year-round weather, although China is catching up in attracting tourists thanks to visa-free schemes, alongside new attractions and cost-effectiveness.
Tour operators are still able to manage their expenses and offer promotions to maintain package prices, she said.
According to the Japan National Tourism Organization, 704,600 Thai travellers visited Japan during the first half of 2026, up 3.5% year-on-year.
If the yen continues to strengthen for a longer period, Mrs Kanlayanee said it may affect the decisions of Thai tourists and their purchasing power.
"Some travellers may reduce their budgets or choose other destinations they view as better value," she said.

items.title: Thailand grants legal work rights to Myanmar refugees with ‘pink cards’
items.summary: NAKHON SAWAN, Aug 6 — Next to a mound of black earth, Myanmar refugees feed soil and rice seed into a clacking con...
items.body_text:
NAKHON SAWAN, Aug 6 — Next to a mound of black earth, Myanmar refugees feed soil and rice seed into a clacking conveyor machine that arranges them into ready-made planting trays for Thai farms.
The farmworkers are among their Thai boss’s newest employees, with a fresh sense of job security after Thailand began permitting Myanmar refugees living in camps to work legally and granting them non-citizen identity cards.
“I do not tire from the work. I can do it,” Ney La Jaw, 25, told AFP.
He spent much of his life confined to the Mae La refugee camp, the largest of nine temporary shelters along the border with Myanmar, according to the United Nations.
But he now lives and works more than 200 kilometres away on a farm in Thailand’s Nakhon Sawan province, earning around 3,000 baht (RM363) per week – a life-changing sum for many refugees.
“I send all of my money home to my mom” in the camp, he said.
After decades of being barred from leaving the camps and working legally, Myanmar refugees and their children began receiving non-citizen Thai ID cards in June, a step away from statelessness and towards gainful, legal employment.
About 4,600 people from Myanmar living in camps have sought permission to work legally from October 2025 to July this year, the Thai interior ministry said.
They are a fraction of the about 80,000 people who have fled conflict-torn Myanmar and live in the camps, according to UN figures.
Myanmar migrants have long toiled in neighbouring Thailand, but the country’s civil war, triggered by a 2021 military coup, has sent even more fleeing across the border.
Myanmar’s leader, ex-junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, arrived in Bangkok on Thursday, with the two nations signing an agreement on labour cooperation.
‘My own future’
In Prachinburi province, AFP journalists saw 15 displaced people collect their new ID cards at a district office in July, smiling and taking photos of the pink documents to send to their families.
“After getting the card, I don’t have to be afraid anymore when travelling around,” said Gay Lah, a Myanmar refugee who fled to a Thai camp with her family at the age of six.
She said her job as a scaffolder was tiring but going smoothly.
“I want to work hard, save money, buy a place, build a house and then bring my family out of the camp, that’s what I imagine,” she added.
Sit Nyein Aye also fled Myanmar as a child and lived most of his life “in misery” in another border camp.
Being allowed to work in construction and having an ID card gave him the chance to start fresh.
“Since I have the opportunity, I’m going out to work,” the 27-year-old said. “I have my own future.”
‘Self-reliance’
The UN refugee agency (UNHCR) welcomed Thailand’s move to issue ID cards in June, calling it a “landmark step towards inclusion, protection and self-reliance for one of the world’s most protracted refugee populations”.
Thailand’s porous borders and reputation for religious and cultural tolerance have long drawn those seeking sanctuary, but Bangkok does not legally recognise refugees or offer asylum.
However, the government began authorising legal employment for longstanding refugees last year, with more than 5,500 refugees joining the workforce since October, UNHCR said in June.
Phil Robertson, director of Bangkok-based Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, said the shift was a “huge step forward” and “long overdue”.
“With these so-called ‘pink cards’, the refugees can access health and other services, work to support their families, and enjoy greater freedom of movement,” he said.
Peace of mind
At the farm in Nakhon Sawan, owner Manas Lohsuwan said he had previously hired Cambodian migrants.
But since deadly border clashes between Thailand and Cambodia broke out in July last year, hundreds of thousands of Cambodian workers have returned home, leaving Manas short of labourers.

items.title: Sanctioned Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing arrives in Bangkok for Asean reintegration talks
items.summary: BANGKOK, Aug 6 — Myanmar’s ex-junta chief Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Bangkok Thursday for his first visit to...
items.body_text:
BANGKOK, Aug 6 — Myanmar’s ex-junta chief Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Bangkok Thursday for his first visit to Thailand as civilian leader, as he seeks a return to the diplomatic fold for his pariah state.
As a general, he led a 2021 military coup that ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war estimated to have killed more than 100,000 people on all sides.
He was installed as Myanmar’s president in April following stage-managed elections that democracy watchdogs and Western nations called a sham intended to launder the junta’s image.
Neighbouring Thailand has since been leading an effort to normalise relations with Myanmar, both bilaterally and through the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
The bloc has excluded Myanmar’s leadership from high-level summits since the putsch, but its foreign minister attended an informal meeting with his regional counterparts last month in Bangkok.
And Min Aung Hlaing has been on a diplomatic drive since swapping his military uniform for civilian dress, visiting India, key ally China, and Asean member Laos in turn.
In the run-up to his Bangkok trip, Suu Kyi – who remains under house arrest – was allowed to meet a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, the first time she has been seen meeting a foreign official since her ouster.
If Myanmar was invited back to Asean, it would open “a pathway for normalisation of relations with others, including western countries that have remained opposed to the military regime”, said Myanmar specialist Morgan Michaels.
But it had already secured recognition from India, China, Russia and Thailand, making restored ties with the regional grouping a “nice to have” rather than essential, he said.
Independent Myanmar analyst David Mathieson told AFP that Myanmar’s campaign for re-entry into Asean was a matter of “pure status” for Min Aung Hlaing.
Myanmar’s leaders have refused to buy into the bloc’s so-called “five-point consensus” to end hostilities through dialogue with all sides.
“He wants to be seen as a responsible member of Asean in one way, then paradoxically to totally reject the five-point consensus,” said Mathieson.
Normalised relations
A source in Min Aung Hlaing’s entourage told AFP he had arrived in Thailand on Thursday, and tracking websites showed a flight from the Myanmar capital Naypyidaw landing in Bangkok.
He is scheduled to be welcomed by an honour guard at Bangkok’s Government House and then meet one-on-one with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, a Thai official told AFP on condition of anonymity.
The Myanmar leader will also attend a business forum and government-hosted dinner, the official said, with the two sides expected to sign a memorandum of understanding on labour cooperation.
Critics say Bangkok should not be rolling out the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing, who has been sanctioned by several Western nations and is wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes against humanity.
But analysts say Bangkok has cause to repair relations.
Fighting between Myanmar’s military and myriad rebel factions has spilled over the long border with Thailand, which hosts millions of refugees from Myanmar.
Thailand also has to deal with the presence of cyberscam networks and illicit drugs traffickers in Myanmar’s volatile borderlands.
Thailand’s Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told reporters on Monday that Thailand believed Myanmar, as well as Cambodia, could “do a lot more” to combat scam networks, and the issue would be raised during Min Aung Hlaing’s visit.
In a statement, he also welcomed Suu Kyi’s Red Cross meeting, saying he hoped that authorities “will undertake further positive steps towards lasting peace and stability in Myanmar”.
Three years ago, Thailand’s then-foreign minister Don Pramudwinai met with Suu Kyi in private for more than an hour, her last known encounter with a foreign envoy since her detention. — AFP

items.title: Iran and Oman agree on new Strait of Hormuz shipping route
items.summary: TEHRAN, Aug 6 — Iran and Oman have agreed a route for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and were finalising ar...
items.body_text:
TEHRAN, Aug 6 — Iran and Oman have agreed a route for ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and were finalising arrangements for jointly managing the strategic waterway, Tehran said Wednesday, even as fresh security incidents highlighted continued risks for regional shipping.
The agreement would be a step towards reopening the key energy route, but official sources briefing Iranian media stressed that any easing still hinged on Washington ending its own naval blockade of Iran’s ports.
Iran has exercised de facto control of the waterway and threatened any vessels transiting routes it deems unauthorised ever since the United States and Israel launched their war against the country on February 28.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly insisted Tehran is keen for a deal to reopen Hormuz, but Iran has denied this and said it will instead make arrangements with its neighbour across the strait, Oman.
“The geographical coordinates of the route envisaged by the two sides have been agreed upon and, if certain third parties do not obstruct the process, the joint statement of the two countries, containing the main considerations and points of agreement, is also in the final review and drafting stage,” Iran foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said, according to state news agency IRNA.
According to the report, Baqaei told journalists that talks with Oman were moving forward, but that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels.
“The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests,” he said.
Highlighting the risks, the captain of an oil tanker reported hearing two explosions while transiting the strait, nine nautical miles (17 kilometres) southeast of Kumzar, Oman, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said on Wednesday. The crew and vessel were safe.
Yemen’s Houthis said separately they had struck two Saudi oil tankers, the eighth and ninth hit since they launched a blockade of the kingdom last month.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said missiles hit the tanker Wafa off Yanbu in the northern Red Sea and the tanker Daisy in the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
‘Fractured system’
Before the war, Hormuz carried around a fifth of the world’s oil and LNG exports, and prices have repeatedly surged since the dispute over the waterway erupted, piling economic and political pressure on Washington.
US Vice President JD Vance acknowledged American frustrations with the pace of diplomacy with Iran, saying negotiations would take time because of divisions within the country’s leadership.
“It’s going to be messy and it’s going to take some time to get there,” Vance told Fox News in an interview broadcast Wednesday.
“The reality... is that number one, the Iranians are extraordinarily difficult people. Number two, they have a fractured system,” he said.
After imposing an effective blockade on the strait, Iran has insisted ships take a route that hugs the Iranian coast.
Many vessels have instead chosen to take a southern route, close to Oman on the opposite side of the strait, occasionally coming under fire.
Iran wants to control the strait and charge tolls, powers it did not exercise before the war and a development that the US would fiercely oppose.
In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran “very hard”, potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back, hinting a deal was near.
But Iran’s foreign ministry denied negotiations were taking place with Washington. — AFP

items.title: Markram returns home from The Hundred for personal reasons
items.body_text:
Markram returns home from The Hundred for personal reasons
Aug 6 : South Africa’s Twenty20 captain Aiden Markram has returned home from the Manchester Super Giants due to personal reasons, the English franchise who compete in The Hundred competition have announced.
Markram had captained the Lancashire side in their first five matches of this season’s competition, scoring 50 in his last outing on Sunday as they lost to MI London.
No reason for Markram’s return to South Africa was given in a statement that said: “Everyone at the Super Giants would like to extend our very best wishes to Aiden at this time, and thank him for his contribution to the team during this year’s competition.”
Jos Buttler has taken over as captain and New Zealand international Michael Bracewell will join the team as the replacement overseas player for the rest of the competition.
Markram, 31, plays for all three Super Giants franchises in Lucknow in the Indian Premier League and Durban in the SA20. Last month he was named South African Cricketer of the Year.
(Writing by Mark Gleeson in Cape Town; Editing by Ken Ferris)

items.title: ‘Overkill’: Chinese travellers push back against ‘tacky’ aesthetics taking over scenic spots in China
items.summary: Online backlash reflects a growing demand for authentic experiences among travellers rather than destinations designed for virality, experts say.
items.body_text:
‘Overkill’: Chinese travellers push back against ‘tacky’ aesthetics taking over scenic spots in China
Online backlash reflects a growing demand for authentic experiences among travellers rather than destinations designed for virality, experts say.
SINGAPORE: If you’ve travelled to China recently, you might have noticed some unusual additions to popular scenic spots.
From street signs bearing slogans like “missing you in Chongqing” to rainbow LED lights illuminating ancient cave systems and giant plastic flowers adorning pagodas and temples, kitschy installations are becoming an increasingly common sight across the country - much to the frustration of Chinese travellers.
“When will such decorations (disappear),” remarked a user on Xiaohongshu, who criticised fake roses and heart-shaped decorations she recently saw around the picturesque Baisha Lake in Xinjiang province.
In May, pictures of a giant pink winged heart sculpture in the middle of Qinghai’s Chaka salt lake went viral.
Famed for its crystal blue water and reflective surface, the lake is a major tourist attraction - welcoming more than two million visitors in 2025.
The sculpture had ruined the lake’s natural beauty, netizens said, describing it as “overkill” and “unnecessary”.
“Hold up - why did they put this in the middle of the lake? Wouldn’t a pristine, unobstructed lake look better? I don’t understand this,” wrote a user on Xiaohongshu - with the handle Xin.
Another user by the handle Weiwei said: “What’s the point of taking photos of nature when there’s something ugly in the middle of it?”
Krisa Chen, a 24-year-old student from Hangzhou, had initially planned on travelling to Qufu city in Shandong province this year - best known as the hometown of Confucius.
But after scrolling through photos from various travel vlogs that described local tourist spots as “messy and ugly” - she decided against it.
Pictures and videos showed crowds of tourists dressed in traditional hanfu gowns, posing under neon lights. Performers were also seen parading the streets.
“A centuries-old historic town should allow visitors to experience architectural scale, street textures, local life, craftsmanship, and historical depth,” she told CNA, adding that many places in China were becoming “overcommercialised”.
She pointed to light shows, artificial waterfalls and photo installations being set up at locations just to attract influencers.
“Using all kinds of colourful LED lights makes it garish and flashy (and) really annoying to look at,” she said.
“They (planners) also force lasers onto water scenic areas and cover ancient buildings with LED screens - and it looks “extremely jarring”, Chen said.
“The aesthetics are just terrible.”
WHY AESTHETICS AND AUTHENTICITY MATTER
Aesthetics are becoming increasingly important to many young travellers, according to a survey published on Jun 18 by the state-owned China Youth Daily newspaper.
Many are dissatisfied with what they see as the declining aesthetic quality of domestic tourist attractions, the report said.
More than 1,000 people between the ages of 20 and 40 were surveyed - with an overwhelming 95 per cent encountering tourist spots with "poor aesthetic quality”.
Respondents also criticised the “forced placements” of lights and decorations that disrupt natural landscapes and scenery - describing them as “colour and visual pollution”.
When a plastic installation or props with “little connection to a place” begin to overshadow its landscapes and architecture, “it is no longer just a matter of personal taste”, said Lina Zhong, a professor from Beijing International Studies University (BISU) and director of its Institute for Big Data Research in Tourism.
“It becomes a question of how tourism resources and public spaces are planned and managed,” she added.
But for destinations under financial pressure, adding decor like props or lights “creates an immediate visual focus”, which could lead to more visitors and tourists - and generate online exposure.

items.title: Castaway SpaceX rocket stage crashed into moon: Scientists
items.body_text:
Castaway SpaceX rocket stage crashed into moon: Scientists
NEW YORK: Part of a SpaceX rocket approximately the size of a bus slammed into the moon as predicted, scientists said on Wednesday (Aug 5), after a telescope in Chile captured evidence of a stream of debris.
The collision, which was not intentional, posed no danger to Earth and is expected to have left a lunar crater in its wake that space agencies, including NASA, still hope to document.
Scientists anticipated the Falcon 9 upper stage was going to strike the lunar surface at approximately 6.35am GMT (2.35pm, Singapore time) on Wednesday.
And it did, the European Southern Observatory said on social media on Wednesday, based on observations recorded by its Very Large Telescope.
The telescope "detected spectral lines", the observatory said, which it called "chemical fingerprints" of "sodium and lithium gas in the impact plume lasting for 5-10 minutes after impact".
"The sodium likely originated from the lunar soil, whereas the lithium could come from the rocket itself," the post continued, adding that the team would offer more details following fuller analysis.
Scientific observers had deemed the 8,690kmh crash inevitable.
"I have Sir Isaac Newton's personal assurance that it did indeed hit the moon, there's no way for it to have escaped," Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and space analyst, told AFP.
NASA and its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter probe and South Korea's Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter were planning to take images of the site after impact, but it could take days to receive that information.
Linking to the European Southern Observatory's post, Benjamin Fernando of Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico told AFP: "I can confirm that the impact did occur."
Fernando was the lead author of a recent paper on the anticipated impact, which had estimated the spacecraft weighed approximately 4,000kg on impact, assuming all of its propellant was spent.
Prior to the collision, NASA had emphasised that "there is no danger to Earth".
"NASA scientists are planning to collect lunar data from the event and refine techniques for tracking objects in space," the United States agency said.
"SPACE JUNK"
The Falcon 9 rocket from Elon Musk's SpaceX launched in January 2025 carrying two lunar landers. Its booster returned to Earth, but the upper stage stayed in space to push the landers onward.
Generally on such missions, SpaceX performs a manoeuvre to make sure the second stage "is safe per the appropriate rules and regulations", said Julianna Scheiman, director of NASA Science and Dragon Programs at SpaceX, at a Monday news conference.
"We did that," she continued, but "what has happened is essentially a mixture of solar activity and gravity forces have put it on a path towards the moon".
Space-trackers like Bill Gray knew it would be tough to observe evidence of the impact from Earth.
"Admittedly, about what we expected" played out in that regard, he told AFP. "But it would have been very nice to be proven wrong, and entirely possible."
NASA hopes to soon establish a sustained human presence on the moon, making it critical to better understand space debris in lunar orbit.
The rocket stage had been just one of tens of thousands of pieces of "space junk" orbiting Earth.
The moon routinely weathers impact from space debris, including meteoroids. Artificial collisions are less common.
In the 1970s, the US space agency carried out deliberate crashes during its Apollo program to collect seismic data.
Some experts have warned that amassing too much space junk around Earth could lead to a dangerous chain reaction of collisions known as the "Kessler syndrome".

items.title: Iran says agreement on Strait of Hormuz shipping reached with Oman
items.summary: The deal now rests on how “third parties” will react to it, says Tehran.
items.body_text:
Iran says agreement on Strait of Hormuz shipping reached with Oman
- Negotiations between the two countries were “forward-moving”, and a deal would be struck “if certain third parties do not obstruct this process”, says Tehran.
- The deal is described as a temporary route lasting two to four months, dependent on changes in US response, and is not a full reopening.
- The ongoing conflict and negotiations impact global oil prices and US politics, with uncertainty remaining over broader peace talks and shipping safety.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran said it reached an agreement with Oman on a proposed route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a potential step toward a reopening of the critical waterway for energy supplies.
A joint statement from Tehran and Muscat is under review and in the final drafting stage, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei told reporters on Aug 5.
Negotiations between the two countries were “forward-moving”, and a deal would be struck “if certain third parties do not obstruct this process”, he said.
Iran and Oman have been in discussions for several days about a management plan for the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as the focal point of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran.
Baghaei did not mention any role of Washington in its statement, except to say the closure of the strait was a result of attacks by the US and Israel.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the announcement.
US President Donald Trump said late on Aug 4 that a deal on the Strait of Hormuz is imminent. He has repeatedly claimed diplomatic breakthroughs in the past, only for a lasting agreement to prove elusive.
Oil steadied on Aug 5 amid mounting signs that the strait might be reopened, potentially restoring production of millions of barrels a day disrupted by the five-month conflict. Brent crude traded around US$79 (S$101) a barrel.
Iran’s latest announcement on Hormuz comes after months of deadlock between the US and Tehran over how to conclude the war, with control over shipping through the waterway a particular sticking point.
Tehran has demanded that vessels obtain permission to cross and pay fees to transit, and has attacked ships it deems to be in violation. The US, in turn, has blockaded Iranian ports.
The issue led to the collapse of a ceasefire and interim peace agreement in July.
While fighting between the sides has paused for now, a number of other issues remain unresolved – not least Iran’s nuclear programme – and there has not been an agreement to start formal negotiations.
Just a ‘temporary’ deal
Iranian state TV earlier played down the outcome of the Iran-Oman discussions, citing a person familiar with the matter as saying an agreement between Tehran and Muscat would not necessarily mean the strait would open immediately. That would be contingent “on a change in US behaviour”, according to the report.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state-run IRNA that Iran and Oman were negotiating a “temporary route” that would remain active for two to four months, with a significant portion of traffic passing through Iran’s territorial waters.
“This understanding does not mean the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
In a Fox News interview recorded on Aug 4, Trump repeated a threat that if Iran does not “make a deal, it’s going to be too bad”.
Over the weekend, he held off on attacks he said would have been the largest since World War II.
Trump told reporters in Los Angeles late on Aug 4 that talks with Iran are “moving along very nicely”, adding: “We’ll know in 48 hours.”
Iran’s stance on Hormuz has complicated Trump’s efforts to turn the page on a war – now in its sixth month – that he claimed would only take weeks.
Shipping disruptions in Hormuz raised energy prices globally and pose a particular threat to Trump and his Republican Party at home, where American voters are already feeling pinched by high costs of living ahead of November midt

items.body_text:
Congo bans exports of copper, cobalt concentrates, official order says
KINSHASA, Aug 6 - Congo has banned exports of copper concentrate and cobalt concentrate in a major escalation of its drive to force domestic processing and retain more value from its vast mineral resources, according to a new government order reviewed by Reuters on Thursday.
The June 29 order, signed by Mines Minister Louis Kabamba Watum, Foreign Trade Minister Julien Paluku Kahongya and Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba, states that "the export of copper and cobalt concentrates is prohibited."
Democratic Republic of Congo, the world's largest cobalt producer and second-largest copper supplier, also introduced a new tax regime for economically significant mining by-products as part of a broader effort to increase revenue from its mining sector.
The ban takes effect immediately, while the new by-product tax regime has a three-month transition period. The mines minister may grant one-year export waivers under "strategic" circumstances, the order said.
Major operators in Congo include China's CMOC, the world's largest cobalt producer, Glencore, Huayou Cobalt, Zijin Mining, Ivanhoe Mines and Eurasian Resources Group. REUTERS

items.body_text:
Sweden’s top court clears way for transfer of seized ship to Ukraine
- Sweden’s top court upheld a ruling to transfer the seized cargo ship Caffa to Ukraine amid suspicions of illegal grain transport from Russian-occupied territory.
- The vessel was seized in March near southern Sweden on suspicion of using a false flag and failing maritime safety laws over poor seaworthiness.
- Ukraine views the case as part of a war crimes probe over property removal from occupied areas; the decision by Sweden’s supreme court is final.
AI generated
STOCKHOLM - Sweden’s top court said on Aug 6 it has upheld a ruling that a cargo vessel seized in the Baltic Sea in 2026 can be handed over to Ukraine, where it is suspected of illegally transporting grain from Russian-occupied territory.
The supreme court dismissed an appeal from the owners of the Caffa vessel, which was seized in March off southern Sweden on suspicion of sailing under a false flag and of violating maritime and ship safety laws owing to a lack of seaworthiness.
Ukraine has sought the ship as part of a probe into suspected war crimes involving the appropriation and removal of property from Russian-occupied territory.
Lower Swedish courts said those alleged actions could constitute a war crime under Swedish law, meaning Sweden could transfer the vessel and related evidence to Ukraine.
“The Supreme Court does not grant leave to appeal. The Court of Appeal’s decision is therefore final,” the supreme court said in a ruling dated Aug 4.
Most of the 11 crew members on Caffa, which is owned by Caffa Shipping Limited, were Russian, the police said at the time of the seizure. REUTERS

items.title: China announces ‘countermeasures’ after US trade sanctions
items.summary: China announced restrictions on drone exports to the United States and blacklisted six companies on Wednesday in response to trade sanctions imposed by Washington over forced labour and national security concerns. The move comes days after the United States imposed fresh tariffs on China and 59 other countries, adding to a series of recent trade […]
items.body_text:
China announced restrictions on drone exports to the United States and blacklisted six companies on Wednesday in response to trade sanctions imposed by Washington over forced labour and national security concerns.
The move comes days after the United States imposed fresh tariffs on China and 59 other countries, adding to a series of recent trade measures.
The US actions “seriously harm China’s legitimate rights and interests”, a commerce ministry spokesperson said in a statement.
“China can only take necessary countermeasures in response, including strengthening export controls on drones, and their key components and technology to the US.”
Beijing’s measures also include suspending factory follow-up inspections by Chinese certification bodies, blacklisting US compliance testing companies, and launching national security investigations into imports of office printers and copiers, according to the ministry.
It also imposed sanctions on six US businesses, including biotech company Applied DNA Sciences and geoscience research firm Stratum Reservoir, barring organisations and individuals within China from “engaging in relevant transactions, cooperation, or other activities with them”.
The six entities “have assisted and supported illegal US sanctions related to Xinjiang; the nature of their actions is egregious”, the commerce ministry said.
The UN has warned of possible crimes against humanity in Xinjiang region targeting the mostly Muslim Uyghur minority — accusations China vehemently denies.
China’s top trade official He Lifeng expressed “serious concern” to US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a call over the recent restrictions, state news agency Xinhua reported.
China also accused the United States last week of seeking to “suppress” Chinese companies, after Washington banned imports of humanoid and quadruped robots manufactured abroad in a move separate from the new tariffs.
China and the United States spent much of last year embroiled in an escalating trade war but reached a truce when US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last October.
The latest US tariffs against China and other trade partners however have threatened that truce, with Beijing warning Washington against waging a trade war.

items.body_text:
HKFP Lens: 8 compete in Hong Kong ‘Sperm Race’ to highlight declining fertility rates
The cause of the decline in sperm health over recent decades remains unclear. Researchers have pointed to environmental pollutants, poor diets and lifestyles, and excessive environmental heat as possible factors.
Hongkongers gathered at a Japanese wine bar in Central on Wednesday to witness eight men compete in Sperm Race Hong Kong.
The event, which aims to raise awareness of declining sperm quality and promote men’s health, involves sperm being placed on a microscopic track. A graphical representation is then shown to the audience as the sperm “race” towards a fake egg.
Event organisers, who dubbed the competition the “world’s smallest sport,” said on Instagram last week that declining sperm quality affects the health of pregnancies and chances of miscarriage and disease.
The testosterone-fuelled competition, which was attended by several local online influencers, was won by a 19-year-old named Anton.
The first contest was launched in Los Angeles last year. The new Asian edition was hosted by Dick Gay.
An HKFP reporter on the scene was told that the competitors collected samples in a bathroom during the afternoon, and footage of the race was pre-recorded shortly after.
A 2022 study led by Hagai Levine, professor of epidemiology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, showed that sperm counts fell on average by 1.2 per cent each year between 1973 and 2018.
The rate of decline has accelerated to more than 2.6 per cent each year since 2000, according to the BBC. “This [declining sperm count] is a marker of poor health of men, maybe even of mankind… We are facing a public health crisis – and we don’t know if it’s reversible,” he said.
The cause of the decline, however, is unclear. Researchers have pointed to environmental pollutants, poor diets and lifestyles, and excessive environmental heat as possible factors.
The nature of the contest has raised eyebrows among critics. Last September, Guardian columnist Arwa Mahdawi wrote that efforts to highlight reproductive health issues are welcome. However, “[s]perm racing reflects three trends dominating Silicon Valley: a fixation on traditional masculinity; an obsession with treating your body like a machine that can be constantly optimised; and an increased interest in fertility that overlaps with a worrying resurgence in eugenics.”

items.title: ‘Isolated incident’: Hong Kong halts investigation into jailed media tycoon Jimmy Lai’s Next Digital as liquidation proceeds
items.summary: The Hong Kong government has formally closed an investigation into jailed media mogul Jimmy Lai’s Next Digital, the parent company of the defunct newspaper Apple Daily, as the firm undergoes liquidation. The government said in a statement on Wednesday that Financial Secretary Paul Chan had ordered the investigation to be terminated after deciding it was […]
items.body_text:
The Hong Kong government has formally closed an investigation into jailed media mogul Jimmy Lai’s Next Digital, the parent company of the defunct newspaper Apple Daily, as the firm undergoes liquidation.
The government said in a statement on Wednesday that Financial Secretary Paul Chan had ordered the investigation to be terminated after deciding it was “no longer necessary” to continue the probe.
Lai was sentenced to 20 years in prison in February on foreign collusion and sedition charges while six former Apple Daily executives were given jail terms of up to a decade in a landmark national security trial.
Alongside Lai, three Next Digital subsidiaries linked to the operation of Apple Daily were also convicted. The firms were later struck off the city’s Companies Register and declared “prohibited organisations” under the Beijing-imposed national security law.
The government also noted on Wednesday that Next Digital has been undergoing a winding-up process following a High Court order in December 2021, and that it was delisted from the city’s stock exchange in January 2023.
‘Isolated’
Chan, the financial secretary, said Hong Kong’s corporate governance regime remained “sound, efficient and aligned with international standards,” adding that companies in the city generally demonstrated high standards of corporate governance.
“The governance and financial problems of [Next Digital], as well as the unlawful acts committed by its senior officers exploiting corporate vehicles, represented only an isolated incident,” Chan was quoted as saying in the statement.
The finance chief appointed Clement Chan, formerly managing director of accounting firm BDO’s Hong Kong branch, as inspector to probe Next Digital in July 2021. The investigation began weeks after national security police raided the company’s headquarters in Tseung Kwan O.
In September that year, Clement Chan submitted an interim report to the finance chief, who then cited “public interest” in ordering the winding-up of Next Digital.
Separately, the government is seeking to confiscate HK$127 million of Lai’s assets. The government has filed an application to the High Court and a hearing is scheduled for November.
The proposed forfeitures include 15 bank accounts under Lai’s name and the assets of 17 companies linked to the tycoon.
Lai’s jail term is the longest handed down so far for a national security offence. Lai did not appeal.
Hong Kong has plummeted in international press freedom indices since the onset of the 2020 and 2024 security laws. Watchdogs cite the arrest and jailing of journalists, raids on newsrooms and the closure of around 10 media outlets including Apple Daily, Stand News and Citizen News. Over 1,000 journalists have lost their jobs, whilst many have emigrated. Meanwhile, the city’s government-funded broadcaster RTHK has adopted new editorial guidelines, purged its archives and axed news and satirical shows.
See also: Explainer: Hong Kong’s press freedom under the national security law
In 2022, Chief Executive John Lee said press freedom was “in the pocket” of Hongkongers but “nobody is above the law.” Although he has told the press to “tell a good Hong Kong story,” government departments have been reluctant to respond to story pitches.

items.body_text:
Why was a US Yale graduate hounded out of his job promoting Chinese culture?
His supposedly sky-high salary and internship at a conservative think tank sparked online fury and rumours he was a US spy
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded with accusations that he was a spy.
His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua said. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the US, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, the article said.
Kuperman, who also goes by the Chinese name Gu Aihua – “Loving China” – started his first job as an intern live-streamer at the Dunhuang Culture International Communication Centre (DCICC) in April, the article said, adding that he believed the city was a “unique entryway to observing China, understanding China and telling China’s stories.”
On his life in Dunhuang, which for centuries was a stop along the Silk Road, Xinhua’s article is typically rosy. One anecdote describes how he spent 3 hours helping a Dutch tourist find their lost backpack. “Kuperman told the relieved tourist, ‘In China, nothing gets lost.’ The tourist nodded in agreement,” the article reads.
The DCICC’s Instagram account featured Kuperman in three videos in May and June, interviewing participants at the Third World Conference of Sinologists and introducing the city’s famous Crescent Lake.

North Korean people struggling to make a living amid record heat are facing a double and triple crisis. Some collapse from heat illness while working outdoors; others run into robbers while moving at dawn or at night to avoid the heat. With no emergency medical system and public safety breaking down, their lives are at serious risk.
A Daily NK source in North Pyongan province said Tuesday that people in Yomju and Ryongchon counties travel between the city and the countryside to sell vegetables, seasonal fruit and corn. Many have repeatedly collapsed in the street after exposure to the midday heat.
“People who live hand to mouth have no choice but to go outside despite the heat,” the source said. “Their livelihood is cut off the moment they stop working. But the heat has gotten so severe that it’s hard to even breathe. Several people a day are seen suddenly losing consciousness and collapsing in the street.”
The bigger problem is that North Korea has no proper emergency medical system to respond. If people feel unwell, their only real option is to find shade and rest or drink water on their own. If someone loses consciousness and collapses, they depend entirely on the help of passersby, according to the source.
“I’ve also seen several people collapsed on the roadside recently. I joined other passersby to move them into the shade or bring them water,” the source said. “It’s not a state rescue system. It’s ordinary people’s goodwill that’s saving lives.”
“These days I often hear stories about people dying from the heat,” the source continued. “But all the state offers is advice like ‘drink apple juice’ or ‘radish juice helps.'”
Even as the risk of heat illness peaks, people still need to earn a living by any means. Many are moving before sunrise or after sunset to avoid the midday heat. But robbery is thriving under cover of darkness, pushing people into a different kind of danger.
Robberies rise as people move at night
“More people are doing business or carrying goods at dawn or at night because they can’t stand the daytime heat,” the source said. “But robbery incidents targeting those hours are also increasing. It’s a vicious cycle. Trying to avoid the heat exposes people to crime instead.”
Weather is beyond anyone’s control. But complaints toward authorities are growing as even a minimal social safety net fails to function, according to the source.
“People are asking why authorities can’t at least strengthen patrols,” the source said, describing the mood on the ground. “If they can’t properly run ambulances or emergency treatment, they should at least help people move around safely. More and more people are saying, ‘Neither the state nor the weather is helping us.'”

items.title: North Korea expands mandatory HIV testing to service workers
items.summary: North Korea has expanded mandatory HIV testing beyond travelers entering and leaving the country. The policy now covers hotel, restaurant and department store workers who may come into contact with foreigners. It is drawing growing complaints in 2026 over its cost and the social stigma it carries. A Daily NK source in Pyongyang said Monday […]
items.body_text:
North Korea has expanded mandatory HIV testing beyond travelers entering and leaving the country. The policy now covers hotel, restaurant and department store workers who may come into contact with foreigners. It is drawing growing complaints in 2026 over its cost and the social stigma it carries.
A Daily NK source in Pyongyang said Monday that North Korea has required quarterly HIV tests since last year. The tests apply to service-sector workers who interact with foreigners entering the country for trade, business, family visits or tourism. The testing covers hotel, restaurant and department store employees in the provinces as well as Pyongyang, the source said.
Workers must undergo the tests regularly and pay for them out of pocket each time. “Workers have to pay $1 each time they’re tested,” the source said. “Getting a sexually transmitted disease test is uncomfortable enough on its own. Many say it’s hard to understand why authorities test them repeatedly when they don’t even know whether they’ve had contact with a foreigner.”
Women in particular feel a heavy psychological burden simply because they are on the list of workers tested, the source said. They become conscious of negative perceptions from those around them. Many see HIV testing less as a public health measure and more as a procedure that casts suspicion on their private lives.
“Workers say things like, ‘Does AIDS spread through the air?'” the source said. “Or, ‘Why do I have to get tested over someone I just passed by?’ Their aversion comes less from the purpose of the test itself. It comes more from feeling suspected of infection.”
HIV does not spread through everyday conversation, handshakes or simply sharing the same space. But North Korea lacks systematic education on transmission routes and prevention. That gap fuels strong social stigma against HIV testing itself.
State denies any domestic HIV cases
North Korea has long maintained that it has no HIV infections within its borders. Authorities have not explained transmission routes, prevention methods or the need for testing. By broadly designating test subjects based solely on contact with foreigners, they appear to be deepening public confusion and anxiety.
Meanwhile, North Korea continues to tighten quarantine and health screening. The measures target people entering and exiting the country and workers who interact with foreigners. Authorities have strengthened HIV and sexually transmitted disease testing since 2019 for North Koreans returning across the China border. They have since applied similar testing to workers returning from overseas postings.
“The quarterly testing fee has become a new burden for service-sector workers who deal with foreigners,” the source said. “As the number of tests increases, complaints are growing. It’s not just the cost. It’s also the discomfort of feeling suspected of infection.”

items.title: North Koreans turn to underground app for banned information
items.summary: North Korean authorities caught a university student in Hamhung, South Hamgyong province, this July for using illicit software that opens access to unauthorized foreign electronic materials. Demand for outside information is growing beyond simple entertainment, driven by North Koreans seeking research and technical knowledge unavailable through state channels. The software, known as the Ryongaksan Program […]
items.body_text:
North Korean authorities caught a university student in Hamhung, South Hamgyong province, this July for using illicit software that opens access to unauthorized foreign electronic materials. Demand for outside information is growing beyond simple entertainment, driven by North Koreans seeking research and technical knowledge unavailable through state channels.
The software, known as the Ryongaksan Program (named for Ryongaksan, a mountain in Pyongyang), has spread rapidly across North Korea in 2026. Authorities have launched an investigation into the program’s sellers and distribution network.
A Daily NK source in South Hamgyong province said Monday that judicial authorities caught the 21-year-old student in mid-July. He had installed the Ryongaksan Program on his mobile phone in Hamhung. The investigation found he bought the program in Pyongyang for $30. Authorities are now tracking down the seller and the distribution route, the source said.
Judicial authorities confiscated the student’s phone. They also plan to seize funds held in the phone’s e-wallet app, on the grounds that the money was used to distribute unauthorized materials, according to the source.
How the Ryongaksan Program works
The Ryongaksan Program lets users search and view external electronic materials stored within it, even while offline, the source said. North Korean IT technicians are believed to have modified similar overseas programs to fit conditions inside the country. The exact developers and the makeup of the installation files remain unconfirmed.
The program reportedly contains entertainment content alongside a large volume of foreign academic papers and technical materials. It is spreading quickly among university students, graduate students and technicians.
“It’s difficult to write academic papers or learn new technology using only materials provided by the state,” the source said. “So this program has drawn particular attention from university students, graduate students and technicians. It’s popular because it includes materials that are hard to obtain inside North Korea, such as advanced foreign construction technology and specialized agricultural data on fertilizer management for different crops.”
North Korean people generally cannot freely access the internet. Access to domestic intranets such as Gwangmyong and Mirae (North Korea’s tightly restricted, closed-loop domestic computer networks) is also strictly limited in scope and eligibility. Against this backdrop, the spread of the Ryongaksan Program reflects strong internal demand to access quality electronic materials freely, without needing a network connection.
City party threatens legal punishment
The Hamhung city party committee issued a directive on July 18 to institutions, enterprises, working organizations and neighborhood watch units. It warned that individuals who reproduce, sell or distribute state-unapproved books and electronic materials will face strong legal punishment, according to the source.
The city party defined mass reproduction or distribution of unauthorized materials as an anti-state act. It said it would hold the heads of relevant units jointly responsible if such incidents occur, the source said.

items.title: Tax, gambling and migration fights ahead for Labor
items.summary: Parliament is yet to resume but the stage has been set for the political fights set to play out next week.
items.body_text:
analysis
Stage is set for debates on tax, migration and gambling ahead of parliament's return
Thu 6 Aug 2026 at 4:26pm
, updated
Thu 6 Aug 2026 at 4:33pm
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Gina Rushton is filling in for Courtney Gould to get you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Parliament is yet to resume but the battlelines have been drawn for political fights set to play out next week when the winter break ends and the prime minister settles back in after his holiday in Tasmania.
The gambling debate has kicked off, the government is readying to unveil its new immigration policy and the treasurer has been tinkering with his tax overhaul.
On Tuesday night, Jim Chalmers released four pieces of draft legislation with the next round of tweaks to his capital gains tax and negative gearing reforms that passed parliament in late June.
The draft promises to fix what critics have dubbed a "widow's tax" (the loss of existing negative gearing access for people who inherit an investment property from their spouse) and so-called "death tax" (taxing disbursements from discretionary trusts established at death).
Chalmers has said the changes reflect the government's "commitment to consult" on the tax reforms announced in the budget while acting opposition leader Jane Hume wasn't buying it, saying Labor was "still trying to clean up a mess of its own making".
The treasurer will be under pressure next week as the Coalition, One Nation, independent David Pocock and the Greens are planning a joint push to force the abolition of the "widow tax" in the next sitting.
Gambling companies won some, lost a bit more at Senate inquiry
You win some, you lose a bit more if you're one of the gambling companies that appeared at this week's Senate inquiry into Labor's wagering laws.
Representatives from Sportsbet, Tabcorp and Responsible Wagering Australia appeared before the inquiry to defend an industry that made Australians the biggest gambling losers per capita with some $32 billion lost annually, including from pokies, according to an Equity Economics report commissioned by anti-gambling advocates last year.
"Publicity-seeking extremists" was how Australian Rugby League Commission chairman Peter V'landys described the senators leading the inquiry. But the companies spent a decent chunk of time defending their own forms of self-promotion, whether it was answering questions about pictures of children wearing Bet365 shirts, or about gambling ads playing between Disney songs on Spotify.
It was tough going too for the department officials responsible for Labor's legislation, as they appeared unable to provide the basis for advertising restrictions.
The legislation would restrict gambling television ads to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm, with a complete ban during live sport in those hours — but a question about the reasoning behind these time frames was taken on notice.
Former rugby league player Luke Bateman gave evidence about his personal experience losing "tens of thousands of dollars a month" to problem gambling.
Bateman, who last month told Australian Story his gambling meant he could barely afford to feed himself while earning $400,000 playing for the Canberra Raiders, said there was "absolutely zero duty of care" from the gambling companies.
He described being flown interstate for race days where he says he was given alcohol and offered his choice of drugs.
Bateman did not disclose during the inquiry that he had been previously employed in the gambling industry, but on Wednesday confirmed to the ABC he had worked for Southern Cross Bet for six months shortly after he left the NRL. He said he was still struggling with problem gambling and quit the position to go into rehab.

Geelong forced to scrap secret concussion deal with player
Updated ,first published
Geelong have backflipped on a written agreement with a senior player, who has a history of concussion, that waived his legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma.
The Cats were forced to scrap the waiver on Thursday after the AFL revealed it had not approved the arrangement. However, the agreement was ratified by the Geelong board, chaired at the time by current AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond.
The deal was also condemned by the AFL Players Association.
The Geelong player, who has asked not to be named, signed the agreement acknowledging his elevated risk of concussion in 2024.
“The AFL and AFLPA are aware of a complex and unique case in which a Geelong player was cleared as fit to play following an assessment by an AFL concussion panel,” the league said in a statement.
“The player then signed a letter acknowledging the potential risk and sought to waive some potential future legal rights, which was not lodged with or approved by the AFL or the AFLPA.
“Geelong has advised the AFL today that the waiver in the letter will be removed, noting that the player continues to acknowledge potential risks.
“The AFL is satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play.”
Geelong CEO Steve Hocking confirmed the Cats had removed the waiver and said the player had not been directed to medically retire.
“Geelong Football Club acknowledges that the letter signed with one of its players went further than was intended and recognises the absence of the AFLPA in the process,” Hocking said in a club statement.
“At the time, the club was involved in extensive discussions with a player, their family and representative in relation to that player’s concussion history.
“Those discussions, including medical advice from the club’s chief medical officer and the AFL concussion panel, were documented in the letter, signed by the player.”
Hocking said the Cats were not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, nor attempting to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws.
“The club’s focus throughout the process was providing care and support to the player, with the intention to give the player agency in the decision-making process around their own playing career.
“The club always aims to ensure that players are provided with information to enable them to make informed decisions about their careers.”
The letter was approved by the Geelong board under then president Drummond, who made a statement to this masthead on Thursday night.
“This matter was complex, sensitive and very carefully considered by the Geelong board at the time,” Drummond said. “The club has today addressed the reasons for decisions in relation to the player and the appropriate changes it will make going forward.”
A source with knowledge of the deal but who was unable to speak on behalf of the club said the letter had given the Cats a level of comfort that the player had given informed consent and was aware of the risks.
Drummond left the Cats at the end of the 2024 season and is now the AFL chairman.
The source said the player was happy with the support, care and treatment he had been given and wanted to continue his career.
The player has played without issue since and, according to the source, continues to be supportive of the club.

items.title: Texts suggest Angus Taylor ‘paid money to the Reformers … or was refusing to’, Icac inquiry hears
items.summary: Jean-Claude Perrottet, brother of former NSW premier, asked about messages referencing federal opposition leader and factional group ReformersIcac’s spotlight has shone on Dominic Perrottet’s brother – and it won’t be the last we hear from his familyNew South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has been shown text messages which suggest Angus Taylor “had paid some money to the Reformers … or was refusing to”, according to the lawyer assisting the inquiry.Taylor, the federal opposition leader, is not
items.body_text:
New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has been shown text messages which suggest Angus Taylor “had paid some money to the Reformers … or was refusing to”, according to the lawyer assisting the inquiry.
Taylor, the federal opposition leader, is not named in Icac’s allegations and has previously denied making payments to the hard-right factional group the Reformers.
Jean-Claude Perrottet, a member, was on Thursday read text messages sent by Reformer cofounder Christian Ellis in September 2021. Ellis says the group has “zero dollars at the moment” in one message.
Jean-Claude asks why and Ellis replies: “Because Michael O’Hara hates the vax campaign, and Angus Taylor hates Rob.”
The counsel assisting Icac, Juliet Curtin, asked: “That seems to be suggesting that Mr Taylor had paid some money to the Reformers too, doesn’t it, or was refusing to?”
Jean-Claude replied: “It sounds like that’s the suggestion.” Curtin then said: “Do you know anything about that?”
“Look, I’ve heard it come up [at the inquiry], but until that came up, I hadn’t recalled that at all,” the younger brother of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet said.
Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of wrongdoing.
The inquiry has previously heard evidence, including from Reformers cofounder Robert Assaf, that hotelier Michael O’Hara threatened to end an arrangement in which he paid lobbying company Beckington for Reformers factional work after the group adopted an anti-vaccination stance.
Inquiry hears intercepted calls
Late on Thursday, the inquiry heard intercepted phone calls from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif for the first time since the opening day of the inquiry.
The corruption watchdog is examining an allegation that between 2020 and 2023, Nassif and his company Toplace made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif.
They including the damage to the career of former Liberal minister and Baulkham Hills MP David Elliott and the removal of the then building commissioner David Chandler, but the inquiry has yet to focus extensively on the allegation.
On Thursday afternoon, Jean-Claude Perrottet was played three phone calls between him and Nassif in 2021, when he was managing shares for Nassif while working at Medallion Financial.
In one call, Nassif can be heard asking Jean-Claude Perrottet to withdraw “100” from his portfolio to give to “to your brother, to Jeremy or Chris” for “preselection”.
Asked about which brother Nassif was proposing to give $100,000, Jean-Claude Perrottet said he didn’t know.
“I don’t know what he’s talking about, to be honest with you,” he said, rejecting the suggestion the money was to support the Reformers recruitment work, describing the call as “nonsense”.
He was played another call, previously heard on the first day of the inquiry, in which Nassif can be heard to claim that he “fucked him [David Elliott] sideways”, forcing “the boys” to get rid of the former Liberal MP’s seat of Baulkham Hills, and had sent “Castle Hill fucking hundreds of new members”.
Jean-Claude Perrottet described the call, in which he also thanked Nassif for “all the support for the family”, as “nonsensical”.
“That’s a throwaway comment that gets used all the time,” he said of his remark to Nassif about his family, saying he was not aware of Nassif providing financial support to bring new Liberal members to the Castle Hill branch.
He described a third phone call, in which Nassif complained about Chandler, who had been scrutinising his developments for defects, as “crazy talk”.
In the call, Nassif allegedly said he “had been promised that the commissioner will be fucking stopped or chased or fucking done something to him”, asking if Jean-Claude Perrottet “can take a message to Charlie or to Dom, the building commissioner, we need to stop him”, and making a subsequent request to “get Charlie to do something pleas

items.body_text:
Major business groups have urged Labor to suspend its immigration changes and consult further with industry about how to get more skilled workers into the country, amid questions about looming Labor tweaks on permanent migration.
With the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, delaying an anticipated immigration speech by at least one week, some Labor MPs say they are anxious to avoid major changes to the family and humanitarian visa categories, with one urging against “performative reductions” in migration in response to One Nation.
But other Labor sources characterised Burke’s changes as tweaks to existing settings, with an expected focus on enforcement of existing rules and small pruning of various programs.
“Tony’s doing an absolutely fantastic job of ensuring, that our immigration program which is so vital for us economically, vital for our vibrancy … the world’s most successful multicultural nation. But it must be properly calibrated,” said the energy minister, Chris Bowen.
Burke was to deliver a National Press Club address on Thursday about migration policy, but withdrew on Tuesday with a spokesperson telling media “some elements of the speech would not be finalised” in time.
The ABC reported measures could include tougher family visa rules, capping backpacker numbers, or restrictions on asylum seekers. Burke’s office would not confirm media reports, and senior sources in the government remained tight-lipped on the changes.
Some sources said they believed media and stakeholder focus on Burke’s speech had been overegged, characterising the changes as more “surgical” adjustments across multiple migration areas, and downplaying major changes to work, family or humanitarian visas.
Another Labor source said they expected Burke’s speech would focus on how Labor plans to cut permanent migration to 185,000 a year – a target the government has cited in budget papers – rather than any cuts below that number.
That figure includes about 132,000 skilled migration places and 52,000 partner and family visas.
But potential cuts to either stream are already facing pushback from business groups and government members.
Outside what will be detailed in Burke’s speech, his department recently announced that skilled migrants who were already in Australia would be given priority for permanent residency, which could help lower total migrant numbers, but also decrease the pipeline of available workers.
The Minerals Council of Australia called on the government to “suspend skilled migration changes and consult industry” more closely on those changes.
The MCA chief executive, Tania Constable, said the reforms would “make it harder for mining and other sectors”, raising fears about skills shortages and risks to project timelines, earnings and the economy. She said mining companies were already struggling to find workers.
“Demand from these sectors for specialised skills is already growing faster than migration pathways can adapt, and industry is frustrated and impeded by slow updates, credential barriers and settlement constraints,” Constable said.
The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, denied rumours of a disagreement with Burke in a cabinet meeting on Monday.
“Migration obviously plays a really significant part in our economy, but it needs to happen at a sustainable rate,” he said.
Pauline Hanson told News 24 that she didn’t care if employers groups thought a migrant crackdown “is going to affect their businesses”.
“I don’t care. My concern is for those Australians that can’t get a roof over their head,” she said.
Labor MP Jerome Laxale told the ABC that Labor would strive to meet its 185,000 permanent migration target.
“If that requires tweaks to our policy to do so, we just have to do that,” he said.

Returning to the NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny, Jean-Claude Perrottet has been asked about messages read out on the first day of the inquiry.

Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asks if the messages are “because it wasn’t money that you or he were being paid for any work that you were doing for Catholic Schools NSW?”

Curtin: “Why is he, why is he calling it filthy schools money?”

Curtin: “OK, well then, if it was just a joke and he’s having a crack, why do you then respond quickly: ‘Don’t put that in writing’?”
Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Why would I want that in writing?”

Almost 600 childcare services were shut down in the latest quarter, a twentyfold increase on the same quarter last year, as federal, state and territory governments crack down on dodgy and underperforming providers.

The Labor MP Jerome Laxale, chair of the committee, says the two groups have confirmed they will attend the next public hearing on 21 August as the inquiry continues:
Transparency is one of the pillars of our democracy, and voters deserve to know who is involved in campaigning at our polling booths.
I thank the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church and Advance for confirming their upcoming attendance to provide evidence to the Committee as we further consider these important issues.
