When Israel was established in 1948, these terrorist organisations, along with their members and leaders, merged into what is now known as the Israeli army.
Rights denied
By 1948, through terrorism and violence, Israel had already colonised 78 percent of historical Palestine. Less than two decades later, particularly during the Six-Day War in 1967, Israel colonised the remaining Palestinian territories: the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
Israeli commanders viewed this as completing the work left unfinished in 1948. The expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has continued uninterrupted since 1967, even during the so-called “peace process” with the Palestine Liberation Organisation.
For typical mainstream Israelis and Zionists, Israel must be a purely Jewish state that controls all Palestinian land. Naturally, the West Bank is no exception in this regard. Zionist theorists find it largely ridiculous to imagine Israel, or the so-called Greater Israel, without a complete subjugation and full colonisation of the West Bank.
Classical Zionist theorists denied the existence of the Palestinian nation long before the establishment of Israel
Legally speaking, Israel has never recognised its military control and colonisation of the Palestinian territories as an occupation, claiming that these territories - Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem - are disputed zones, where Palestinians are just residents, not citizens.

Over the past decade, Israel has significantly increased its illegal confiscation of Palestinian land and settlement expansion. Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are some the latest updates from across the region:
- 
	US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that Washington is holding talks with Tehran and would prefer an agreement over further military action against Iran. "I would rather make a deal with Iran because I don’t want to kill people," he said during an event in in Las Vegas.
- 
	A tanker 9 nautical miles south east of Oman's Kumzar reported hearing two blasts while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said early on Thursday. The vessel and its crew were reportedly safe, with no environmental damage indicated.
- 
	US President Donald Trump clashed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Washington's critical munition shortage during the war on Iran, The Washington Post reported. During the meeting, Hegseth reportedly defended himself and instead blamed Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg for the weapon depletion and "for not ensuring Trump was fully apprised" about the state of Washington's stockpiles.
- 
	The US army has used up nearly 80 percent of its interceptors for a key missile defence system, CNN reported citing several sources. Senior US military officials warned that the Pentagon’s munitions stockpile is "dangerously low," with key air defence systems particularly depleted during the war on Iran.
- 
	Donald Trump has hit back on media reports of depleting munitions, insisting that the army has "massive amounts of 'munitions'" and expanding manufacturing. He also threatened that "'leakers' of these treasonous statements are being hunted down," and wrote that "long term jail sentences will be sought".
- 
	Israeli reports are suggesting that there are considerations for additional military attacks in Lebanon, as the army prepares for further escalation in the country despite ongoing peace talks. This comes amid Lebanon's state-media reporting of escalating Israeli attacks, which left at least four wounded over the past few hours.

items.title: Ebola crisis deepens in DR Congo as cases surge in hotspots
items.summary: This outbreak, caused by the **Bundibugyo virus**, has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded and the fastest-spreading in Congo’s history.
items.body_text:
Democratic Republic of Congo
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is accelerating, with health officials warning that cases are doubling in some of the hardest-hit areas.
On Wednesday, World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met with President Félix Tshisekedi in Kinshasa, marking his second visit to the country since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.
Tedros, accompanied by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director-General Jean Kaseya, said the situation remains deeply concerning as transmission continues to rise.
According to Congo’s Ministry of Health, the outbreak has now recorded 3,874 confirmed cases and 1,751 deaths.
The United States announced an additional 242 million dollars in funding for emergency Ebola response, preparedness, and humanitarian support across the region.
This outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded and the fastest-spreading in Congo’s history. With no approved vaccine or treatment for this strain, health authorities are racing to contain the virus and prevent further loss of life.

items.title: FIFA backs embattled president Infantino following crisis meeting
items.summary: FIFA also apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over the now-shelved proposal to open the World Cup to private investment.
items.body_text:
FIFA
World football governing body, FIFA, has reaffirmed its support for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino, following a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday amid calls for him to resign.
FIFA also apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over the now-shelved proposal to open the World Cup to private investment.
"A review will now be conducted, and a report will be presented to the FIFA Council at its next scheduled meeting," the FIFA statement said.
The controversial plan to sell a 20 per cent stake in a new commercial rights entity provoked a fierce backlash and was withdrawn last Friday.
It also drew fierce criticism because of the involvement of a company with family links to US President Donald Trump.
European football’s powerful governing body, UEFA, termed the proposal to privatise the World Cup a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal" hatched by Infantino.
The FIFA president has been facing increasing pressure, including from two senior FIFA officials, since the proposal was announced, amid growing calls for him to step down.
This backlash raised questions over his re-election as president next March, with both UEFA and Americas’ CONCACAF football body saying they had lost confidence in him.
The North and Central American governing body called for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency" while slamming Infantino's "poor governance and leadership".
The association of European soccer leagues, including the Premier League, La Liga, and Serie A, on Wednesday called for a reform of governance at the world body.
“Now more than ever, FIFA requires governance reform that ensures that all relevant stakeholders have a formal role in decisions that shape the future of our game,” they said.
European Leagues hit out at the possibility of further expanding the World Cup to 64 teams and said “FIFA must not be allowed to continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions”.
It said that until there was reform it would reject the “expansion or creation” of FIFA competitions.
Also on Wednesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose country co-hosted the 2026 World Cup with the US and Mexico, said he no longer had confidence in Infantino's ability to lead FIFA.
He had been expected to stand unopposed for a fourth and final term in office at the March elections.
But Infantino still has plenty of allies, particularly in parts of the world where poor associations rely on FIFA's largesse to operate.

items.title: Uganda football star David Owori killed in suspected robbery

items.body_text:
Uganda
Ugandan footballer David Owori has died after being attacked during what police believe was a robbery near his home in the capital, Kampala.
The 27-year-old, who captained SC Villa and represented Uganda's national team, suffered serious injuries after reportedly resisting an attempt to steal his phone and other valuables. He was taken to hospital but later died.
Police have launched an investigation and say officers are working to identify the attackers.
Owori's death has triggered an outpouring of grief across Uganda, with teammates, fans and political leaders paying tribute to one of the country's most respected footballers.
SC Villa described him as "a leader, brother and friend", while the Federation of Uganda Football Associations (FUFA) praised his influence on and off the pitch.
Owori returned to SC Villa in 2023 and helped the club win the Uganda Premier League title in 2024, ending a 20-year wait for the championship. His performances also earned him a contract extension until 2027.
The killing has also renewed concerns about violent crime in Kampala, with many Ugandans calling for stronger action against criminals.
It comes just weeks after Ugandan rugby international Sydney Gongodyo was killed in a separate attack in the city.

items.title: FIFA apologises over investor plan, backs Infantino despite backlash
items.summary: FIFA’s leadership made a hesitant and unconvincing retreat after Infantino was forced to drop his privatisation scheme.
items.body_text:
Under heavy criticism following its abandoned plan to open up to private investors, FIFA’s leadership acknowledged that “mistakes” had been made and issued an “apology”, while nevertheless reaffirming its “full support” for President Gianni Infantino on Wednesday after a crisis meeting in Morocco.
The meeting, which was closed to the press, took place at FIFA’s African headquarters within the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Salé, near Rabat.
Late in the evening, FIFA’s leadership released a statement acknowledging “that mistakes were made following the leak of the proposal to the media”. It added that “an apology was offered for those mistakes, together with a commitment to ensure that they are not repeated”.
“It was agreed that there had never been any intention to exclude the FIFA Council and FIFA member associations from the process, and that the matter should have been handled differently,” the statement admitted, without mentioning Infantino by name.
“In this particular case, however, it is important to emphasise that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done complied fully with FIFA’s regulatory framework,” it added.
Senior officials rallied behind Infantino, who has come under sustained criticism in recent days.
“The members of the FIFA Governing Council present reaffirmed their full support for Infantino as the only official elected by FIFA’s 211 member associations,” the statement said.
FIFA ‘will no longer tolerate any attack’
“Now that the project has been abandoned, it is understood that FIFA will no longer tolerate any attack on its integrity, good governance or due process, and that it will take all necessary measures to protect and preserve its name and reputation,” the statement continued.
Infantino, who has faced criticism from some of his closest associates, appeared willing to draw a line under the affair. He reiterated “his full support for FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström and the FIFA administration for their indispensable and outstanding work in implementing his vision”.
In a letter to FIFA employees seen by AFP, Grafström had expressed regret over “a series of sad and unacceptable events”.
Infantino, who attended Wednesday evening’s Women’s Africa Cup of Nations match between Zambia and Malawi in Rabat, has led world football’s governing body for 10 years. The Italian-Swiss official has launched a succession of divisive initiatives, culminating last week in the announcement of plans to establish an external company (FIFA Forward Enterprise, FFE) to manage FIFA’s commercial activities and tournaments such as the World Cup, with the participation of private investors.
I have no confidence in Infantino after what has happened
The proposal, which came as a surprise when it was revealed by the media last Tuesday, was ultimately withdrawn overnight from Friday to Saturday following opposition from numerous stakeholders in football, including European governing body UEFA.
Several senior FIFA figures have distanced themselves from Infantino in recent days, including Arsène Wenger, the organisation’s Chief of Global Football Development.
Infantino’s senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned on Friday, saying he was “categorically opposed” to the proposal.
Political pressure
On Wednesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney joined British counterpart Andy Burnham in criticising the FIFA president.
“I have no confidence in Infantino after what has happened,” Carney said. “The idea that good governance means withholding information from your closest advisers (…) is fatal.”
On Friday, Burnham said Infantino was “the wrong person to lead” FIFA.
Within football, pressure has come from both UEFA and Concacaf (the governing body for North America, Central America and the Caribbean).

items.title: Are India and Indonesia Leaving the Non-Aligned Movement Behind?
items.summary: Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions.
items.body_text:
When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Jakarta last month, the joint statement issued by India and Indonesia addressed almost every major strategic issue facing Asia. It highlighted the Indo-Pacific, BRICS, ASEAN, maritime security, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, resilient supply chains, and cooperation among the Global South. Yet there was no reference to the Non Aligned Movement (NAM), despite India and Indonesia being among its founding members and the leaders whose cooperation at the 1955 Bandung Conference helped lay its intellectual foundations.
The NAM was similarly absent from the joint statement issued during President Prabowo Subianto’s visit to India in January 2025. The disappearance of the NAM offers a window into how two of Asia’s most important middle powers now understand strategic autonomy. Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions, partnerships, and diplomatic priorities.
India and Indonesia have long occupied a unique place in the history of postcolonial diplomacy. The Bandung Conference articulated principles of sovereignty, anti-colonialism, peaceful coexistence, and independent foreign policy that later shaped the establishment of the NAM in 1961. During the Cold War, these ideas provided newly independent states with a framework for resisting pressure to align with either Washington or Moscow while asserting a greater voice in international affairs.
But the strategic environment that gave rise to non-alignment no longer exists. The central challenge facing Asian middle powers today is not simply avoiding military blocs. It is preserving policy autonomy while navigating an increasingly complex landscape shaped by great power competition, economic interdependence, technological rivalry, and overlapping regional institutions. Strategic autonomy has therefore become less about standing apart from the international system than about participating in it on one’s own terms.
That evolution is clearly reflected in the India-Indonesia partnership. Rather than centering the relationship on the language of non-alignment, the two countries frame their cooperation through a dense network of contemporary frameworks, including ASEAN, BRICS, the G20, the Indian Ocean Rim Association, and overlapping conceptions of the Indo-Pacific. In building up their ties, India and Indonesia have placed equal emphasis on defense industrial cooperation, maritime domain awareness, artificial intelligence, digital connectivity, critical minerals, and resilient supply chains. These priorities represent a different way of pursuing national resilience and strategic flexibility. Strategic autonomy has become increasingly issue-based rather than institution-based.
During the Cold War, the NAM served as the principal political vehicle through which many developing countries expressed their independence. Today, India and Indonesia pursue the same objective across multiple platforms simultaneously. ASEAN reinforces regional diplomacy. BRICS expands cooperation among emerging economies. The G20 provides influence over global economic governance. Indo-Pacific initiatives address maritime security and connectivity. Rather than relying on a single movement, both countries increasingly assemble strategic autonomy through overlapping partnerships.
Importantly, the principles associated with Bandung – sovereignty, territorial integrity, international law, peaceful dispute settlement, and a stronger voice for the Global South – have not disappeared. These are ideas deeply embedded in the diplomatic traditions of both countries, but those principles are now expressed through different means.
This distinction matters beyond India and Indonesia. Across Asia, middle powers are adapting to a strategic environment that is simultaneously more interconnected and more contested than the Cold War order. Few seek exclusive alignment with any si

items.title: Has Life in North Korea Changed Since 2013?
items.summary: The author of “Witness to North Korea” reflects on which lessons from his time in the country are still relevant today.
items.body_text:
Last month, as I launched my new book “Witness to North Korea,” conversations with Wall Street Beijing Bureau Chief Jonathan Cheng and NK News’ Alannah Hill brought up one important question: is this memoir of my three years living and working as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) still relevant to the North Korea of today?
I wrote this book for anyone wishing to understand, as Stimson Center Fellow Frank Aum wrote, “what it actually means to engage with the DPRK – not in the abstract language of policy briefs, but through the granular, often maddening, reality of day-to-day diplomacy and humanitarian work.”
This question of continued relevance between what I observed then and the country today is a valid one. After all, I left Pyongyang in 2013 – and yes, things in the country have changed since my departure. Some North Korea experts talk of a rising middle class with cash to spare, of one mobile phone subscriber for every three North Koreans, of ski resorts – all thanks to the phenomena of marketization and monetization changing the up-to-now closed economy and forcing the hand of the North Korean regime to open to international trade.
Another thing has changed: data has become even harder to obtain. In 2020, North Korea used the COVID-19 pandemic to deny entry to several EU-member countries that had kept an embassy in Pyongyang and to most of the international community’s assistance programs. These embassies and resident U.N. agencies, as well as most international NGOs, have not yet returned. The U.N. population census remains, to this day, an essential source of quality data about North Korean society. Sadly, there has not been such an exercise since I left 13 years ago.
My discussions with U.N. officials and humanitarian organizations point, today, to a continuation of the underlying problems that I describe in my book, which continue to shape the lives of ordinary North Koreans. Kim Jong Un’s regime continues to experience a gap between intention and reality in four major areas: food and nutrition; public health and infectious disease; availability of medicines and medical equipment; and, finally, technical cooperation and capacity building. These problems concern both domestic limitations and international constraints.
During my years in Pyongyang, the United Nations and many NGOs worked with North Korean institutions to improve agricultural production, strengthen health services, support maternal and child nutrition, conduct the national population census, and assist vulnerable communities facing chronic shortages. These efforts were based on a simple reality: despite its political isolation, the North Korean population faced genuine needs that could not be solved through sanctions or diplomacy alone.
Kim Jong Un’s unusually candid admission last February that agricultural production remains inadequate and that decades of rural policy have failed echoes many of the concerns that humanitarian agencies encountered during my posting. While today the emphasis has shifted toward livestock production, dairy farming, and regional development, the objective remains the same: providing sufficient and nutritious food to a population that continues to experience chronic shortages.
During my time in North Korea, workplaces and factories would allow their people to leave during the day to forage in the hills, as the government acknowledged the persistence of a “food problem.” Today, the North Korean government’s ambitious rural modernization program reflects an acknowledgement that food security is still a national challenge rather than a problem of the past.
The health sector presents an equally familiar picture. items.title: When the World Stops Fearing the Bomb
items.summary: On the 81st anniversary of the bombing of Japan, the hibakusha are disappearing just as fast as the world is becoming numb to their cause
items.body_text:
Terumi Tanaka was 13 when on one fine day the sky above Nagasaki was suddenly flooded with blinding white glare; “a blazing inferno” he would recall years later. At 97 now, he still carries memories of sitting next to the window. His home was hit suddenly by a flash, then thunder, followed by an unbearable silence. Within moments, his city was reduced to ash.
“It was literally hell,” he said in his eyewitness account.
With the average age of the hibakusha (atomic bombing survivors) reaching 87, there will soon be no one left to provide such first-person testimony.
As humanity loses these eyewitnesses — 91,105 left as of March 2026 — we are also losing our moral compass. As the world commemorates the 81st anniversary of the dropping of atomic bombs on Japan, a cruel irony is fast unfolding in front of our eyes. The generation that witnessed the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings is fading away just as the world rediscovers the strategic significance of nuclear weapons — and loses sight of the human suffering such weapons embody.
For decades, the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki had imposed an invisible restraint on policymakers. Nuclear weapons were tolerated, but never celebrated. The nuclear taboo — non-possession, non-transfer, and non-use of nuclear weapons — was assumed to be universal and robust. Today, deterrence has displaced disarmament as the dominant concern. Even before the last hibakusha leave this earth, the world is turning its back on their warnings.
The Return of the Bomb
The nine nuclear-armed states possess 12,241 nuclear warheads, with nearly 9,614 retained in military stockpiles. This is certainly better than 70,300 warheads in 1986 when Russia and the United States possessed more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear bombs. Driven by their detente of 1970s and the end of Cold War from late 1980s, the Soviet-U.S. (and later Russia-U.S.) arms control agreements had really shrunk their arsenals. But with all nuclear-armed states now busy with modernizing their nuclear weapons, that trajectory of arms control has begun to reverse.
China has expanded its stockpile the fastest: from 350 warheads in 2022 to 620 in January 2026. The United States and Russia are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in next-generation delivery systems. Britain plans to raise its warhead ceiling, while France is upgrading its sea-based deterrent. More worrying still, nuclear doctrines are lowering the threshold for potential use. In India, where it was long assumed that its warheads stayed de-coupled from their launchers, SIPRI this year reported that 12 nuclear warheads had been actively deployed as its sea-based deterrent. Nuclear weapons are no longer regarded as weapons of last resort; they are steadily becoming instruments of routine statecraft.
This transformation marks the collapse of the post-Cold War belief that nuclear weapons were gradually becoming politically less valuable. Instead, great power rivalry, especially since the start of the Ukraine war, has revived the centrality of deterrence discourse. With the expiry of the New START Treaty on February 5, 2026, the United States and Russia no longer have any legally binding bilateral nuclear arms control treaty limiting their nuclear arsenals.
Equally revealing is what has happened to disarmament discourse. The Chemical Weapons Convention, negotiated in the early 1990s, was the last disarmament treaty successfully concluded through traditional inter-state mechanisms. Since then, the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva — the world’s sole standing multilateral negotiating forum on arms control — has remained paralyzed.
Civil society organizations have since stepped in to fill the vacuum. Their efforts produced the Ottawa Convention banning anti-personnel landmines, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, Arms Trade Treaty and, eventually, the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. items.title: Railway can transform Persian Gulf politics and global security
items.summary: The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, wider tensions in the Red Sea and the oil price spikes these circumstances occassion have made one thing abundantly clear: Gulf countries and global markets are dependent on vulnerable maritime routes. But while national leaders and diplomats work to free up crucial waterways through which much of the […] The post Railway can transform Persian Gulf politics and global security appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
The crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, wider tensions in the Red Sea and the oil price spikes these circumstances occassion have made one thing abundantly clear: Gulf countries and global markets are dependent on vulnerable maritime routes.
But while national leaders and diplomats work to free up crucial waterways through which much of the world’s trade passes, another transport phenomenon is tentatively underway. For over 15 years, six Arab Gulf countries have been quietly cooperating to build a railway network – and the project has recently accelerated.
The aim is to increase the Gulf’s economic integration and improve the region’s resilience and security. But as experts of global governance and political economy, we also ask: Could such a rail project help reshape politics and conflict in the region?
That question is especially salient now, given that the US-Iran war has meant months of severely disrupted and largely halted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Putting regional integration on track
Routes in and out of the Persian Gulf region have long been subject to outside influence from military powers and bitter regional rivalries and conflicts. That has included Portuguese control of Hormuz during part of the 16th and 17th centuries, and British and American naval and airpower.
Since the founding of the Gulf Cooperation Council in 1981, leaders of its six member countries – Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – have channeled efforts into regional integration. But despite 45 years of summits and joint declarations, economic and political cooperation has generally lagged behind rhetoric.
The current war in Iran has served to underscore the need for Gulf cooperation, and the GCC Railway project may be the means by which this is finally achieved.
Announced at the 30th summit of the council in 2009, the project aims to build a 1,352-mile (2,177-kilometer) railway network connecting the six GCC states at a projected cost of US$250 billion. The plan envisions standard gauge freight and passenger rail services with speeds between 50 to 60 mph (80-100 kph) for freight and 120 mph (200 kph) for passenger rail, all to be equipped with European train control technologies.
After initially slow progress, mostly due to periods of low oil prices that delayed many investments in the fossil fuel-rich countries, the UAE and Saudi Arabia led an acceleration of the project in the 2020s.
Then came the war with Iran. In April 2026 the GCC leaders gathered in Jeddah in Saudi Arabia amid strikes from Tehran against Gulf states and the crisis closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The gathered kingdoms called for increased security cooperation as well as joint electricity and oil pipeline connections between GCC states. They also pledged expedited construction and completion of the GCC railway project.
With GCC countries responsible for building and operating its section of the project, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have made the most progress to date.
The UAE launched Etihad Rail in June 2026, transporting passengers between Abu Dhabi and Fujairah. A full service line from the Gulf of Oman to the Saudi border is scheduled to open by the end of the year; construction of the UAE-Oman segment is well underway; and Qatar, Bahrain and Kuwait are moving their sections through planning and design processes.
Earlier in 2026 the director of the GCC Rail Authority noted the project had reached 50% completion and is on track to be operational in 2030.
More connections to Europe and Asia
Once completed, the network will create the Gulf region’s first integrated, cross-border rail system, stretching from ports on the Gulf of Oman to Kuwait City.
But even more transformative integration plans are taking shape.
Several potential connections to Europe are under consideration or in development.
The GCC Railway could connect the Gulf of Oman and all six GCC member countries to Europe through several possible routes:
- From Kuwait through Ira

items.body_text:
Valar Atomics, a three-year-old microreactor developer that has a forged a close relationship with the Trump administration, has raised $1 billion in its Series B funding round as investors increasingly bet that the White House’s overhaul of nuclear regulations will clear the way for the country’s first big atomic buildout in more than half a century.
This week, the Torrance, California-based startup announced that its latest funding round, led by venture capital giant Sequoia, will be used to lay the groundwork for commercialization of Valar’s five-megawatt Ward 250 reactor, which uses helium as a coolant instead of water. The reactor design has yet to receive approval from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
“So, what does the new Series B financing mean for Valar? It allows us to make the next mission critical evolution: Valar will transition from demonstrating the operability of an integrated reactor system to producing fleets of them en masse,” Valar founder and CEO Isaiah Taylor said in a post on the company website. “This has been Valar’s mission since its inception.”
It’s a milestone for a company that once drew derision within the nuclear industry over audacious social media claims its 27-year-old founder made to back up a lawsuit against the NRC. The young executive’s showmanship, shrouded in patriotic language, attracted attention from Republican officials. Before long, Valar had emerged as what Mother Jones called “the Trump administration’s favorite nuclear startup.”
Last August, the Department of Energy selected Valar as one of 10 companies to take part in a new pilot program that aimed to help next-generation reactor startups split atoms for the first time. A month later, the agency named the company as one of four to take part in a separate pilot program to develop new supply chains for nuclear fuel. Two months after that, Valar became the first venture-backed startup to split atoms using an experimental core at Los Alamos National Laboratory.
In February, Valar made history by loading the parts for its Ward 250 onto a C-17 Globemaster III aircraft at the March Air Reserve Base in California and flying them to Utah’s Hill Air Force Base. The airlift, touted by the Trump administration as “groundbreaking,” was the first demonstration that a microreactor could be wholly transported by plane. In June, Valar split atoms with its prototype Ward 250, becoming the second company in the pilot program to do so.
The new funding, the company said Monday, will allow it “to fully execute a vertically integrated, hardware first approach; one that encompasses everything from reactor deployment and long-term operations to fuel production.”
The company faces significant hurdles to realize that vision. The US operated what’s known as a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor back in the 1970s. The Fort St. Vrain nuclear station, Colorado’s only such facility, shut down after a decade of costly maintenance issues and outages. It was replaced with a natural gas-fired plant. A handful of similar reactors have been built around the world, but primarily operated as experimental units.
China started construction on its first major high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in 2012, and split atoms for the first time in 2021.
But Beijing really reignited the race to commercialize the technology, which could help avoid tricky questions around using water for cooling, in December 2023. That’s when China’s first 150-megawatt, helium-cooled reactor began selling electricity to the grid.
Two years later, China launched a new industrial alliance to hasten the development of high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. In January, Beijing kicked off construction on its second such reactor, which will have four times the capacity of the first one.

When things go up, the optimists get the panel seats and the magazine covers. items.body_text:
There is a way to work out which direction markets have been moving without looking at a single price. Watch who is handed the megaphone. When things go up, the optimists get the panel seats and the magazine covers. When things turn down, as they have these past few weeks, the bears who had gone quiet reappear with the full folder, and the folder is remarkably well preserved. Most of what is in it has been in it for three years.
Truth be told, some of the contents have quietly gone missing. Nobody talks much anymore about the statistical parrot, or the university surveys proving that nobody uses AI. They were retired without a funeral. In their place has come rapidly growing Chinese innovation, held up as the threat by the same people who, in the following breath, suggest that their favorite champions should stop spending to meet it.
Beneath the newer complaints, chiefly that today’s spending will earn nothing tomorrow, one older fear survives every cycle. It takes a fresh coat of paint each time and reappears the moment the tape turns red. It is the argument about circularity.
The loop diagrams have enormous meme potential, which accounts for half their appeal. The other half is that nobody has been able to dispute the profits of the largest companies, and nobody has produced the forensic report that would settle the matter.
So the suggestion gets made obliquely instead that:
The profits are real, but not the kind that count. A handful of very large companies buy from each other, invest in each other, sign supply agreements with each other and take stakes in each other. Money leaves by one door and returns through another. Sales get booked at both ends.
In the harsher versions, the phrase is wash trade, which describes a transaction where nothing genuinely changes hands and everyone involved is manufacturing the appearance of activity.
Underneath the disagreement sits something more basic, repeated here for the umpteenth time. Technology is no longer a sector where money can be made without money being spent.
For roughly three decades it was, gloriously so, and an entire investing culture grew up around the fact. Ideas built the moats. Facebook, Amazon, Google and Uber did not need a smelter.
That era has closed for most of the large companies, and what replaced it is long-duration capital expenditure, new to technology but about as new to the rest of the world as the wheel. Steel, shipping, refining and airlines have lived on it for a century.
Long-duration capex arrives with a companion that shocks only those who have never met it. Companies in high growth pass through periods of negative cash flow, and even slow-growing ones can go cash-flow negative on a single large project.
This is ordinary. The reaction is not. The first time a technology investor sees a rating come down or a cost of debt go up, the response tends to be closer to shrieking than to analysis. Few have had reason to read anything on rating optimization, and so few know that the companies that organize themselves entirely around protecting the highest grade on their debt are the same companies that reliably miss the opportunities that made the balance sheet worth having.
Which brings back the diagram. Somebody with excellent presentation software reads the news, and every time two companies announce anything, another arrow gets drawn. It has become close to a competition between financial publications over whose illustrators can produce the most fearsome tangle. Add an arrow. Add a logo. Mention Global Crossing, or Enron, in a sentence built so that no name and no accusation ever share a clause.
The implication does the rest. One day the recession arrives, everyone looks inside the boxes and the revenues are not there.
A diagram is not an argument

items.title: Rwanda orders alcohol recall after deadly poisoning
items.summary: Rwanda has recalled alcoholic drinks nationwide after contaminated liquor killed at least 50 Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Rwanda orders alcohol recall after deadly poisoning
Rwanda has ordered a nationwide recall of alcoholic beverages and shut down 101 manufacturing facilities following a wave of deaths and illnesses linked to contaminated liquor.
The Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority (Rwanda FDA) announced the measures on Monday after inspections uncovered widespread safety and licensing violations at different distilleries. The recall affects dozens of locally produced alcoholic beverages.
At least 50 people have died this year after consuming contaminated liquor, while more than 500 required hospital treatment and around 100 reportedly suffered blindness, according to Rwanda’s health ministry.
“We consider it an epidemic,” Health Minister Sabin Nsanzimana said, as quoted by local media, warning that the country would “pay the price tomorrow” without urgent action.
The crackdown comes amid widespread alcohol consumption in Rwanda. The Seventh Rwanda Demographic and Health Survey found that 15% of men and 7% of women drink alcohol daily, while half of men and 18% of women aged 15 to 49 surveyed had consumed alcohol in the preceding month.
Rwanda’s campaign mirrors a broader regional push to curb alcohol abuse. In neighboring Kenya, authorities launched a nationwide crackdown in 2024, shutting down thousands of illegal bars and distilleries, tightening licensing rules and introducing tougher penalties for venues that violated operating hours.
Uganda has also stepped up efforts to tackle alcohol abuse, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO), which has backed new national guidelines for treating alcohol use disorders.
The WHO has also said European colonial expansion transformed alcohol in Africa from a largely local product into a commercial commodity through taxation and mass distribution.
In a review, the agency noted the colonial period “introduced commercialization and taxation of alcoholic beverages” and used alcohol availability as a tool to control local workforces.
items.normalised_title: rwanda orders alcohol recall after deadly poisoning

items.title: El Nino presents acute hunger threat to 49 million people – UN
items.summary: More than 18 million people in eastern and southern Africa face food insecurity triggered by El Nino, the World Food Programme has said Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
El Nino presents acute hunger threat to 49 million people – UN
The unprecedented strengthening of the El Nino in the Pacific Ocean could force at least 49 million people into acute food insecurity worldwide in 18 months, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) has warned.
This year’s “extremely anomalous” El Nino is set to surpass the existing record level by almost 25%, severely disrupting rainfall and harvests.
More than 18 million people in eastern and southern Africa will be at risk of food insecurity. Countries in the south of the continent are particularly exposed because many households there depend on rain-fed subsistence agriculture, the agency warned on Wednesday.
The projection would raise the number of people facing crisis-level food insecurity or worse across 45 vulnerable countries from approximately 225 million to 274 million – an increase of 22%. Central America and southern Africa are expected to suffer the greatest effects, while eastern Africa and South and Southeast Asia could also experience significant disruption.
El Nino, the warming phase of a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific, can cause severe drought in some regions and destructive flooding in others. The current event is expected to peak between September and December 2026, although its effects on harvests could continue throughout 2027.
“The sooner we help families to prepare for these climate shocks, the greater our ability to save lives and protect livelihoods,” WFP Acting Executive Director Carl Skau said.
The warning comes as southern Africa continues to recover from the 2023-2024 El Nino, which produced the region’s worst mid-season dry spell in more than a century and its lowest mid-season rainfall in 40 years, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe declared drought-related emergencies or disasters, while more than 30 million people across southern Africa required humanitarian assistance, according to OCHA.
Russia has also provided food assistance to countries affected by the regional crisis. In 2024, Moscow donated 25,000 metric tons of wheat to Zimbabwe and funded WFP deliveries of sunflower oil and pulses. It provided Zambia with $2 million in food aid through WFP in December 2025, the Russian Foreign Ministry reported.
The WFP said on Wednesday it has activated anticipatory programs in South Sudan, Chad, Mauritania, Uganda, Guatemala, and El Salvador since May, providing more than $14 million to around 500,000 people.
However, humanitarian agencies face funding shortages that could limit their ability to respond. Richard Choularton, director of the WFP’s Climate and Resilience Service has said some food-security data collection has been curtailed because of insufficient funding.
In June, the WFP and the Food and Agriculture Organization launched a $202 million appeal to protect 8.8 million people in 22 countries – more than half of them in Africa. According to the appeal, the agencies are positioned to support 1.2 million people but need another $167 million to reach an additional 7.6 million.

items.title: Russia delivers food aid to war-torn Mali
items.summary: Russia has delivered 770 tons of food aid to Mali, with the WFP saying the shipment will help more than 57,000 vulnerable people Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Russia delivers food aid to war-torn Mali
Russia has delivered 770 metric tons of food aid to Mali, Moscow’s embassy in Bamako announced on Tuesday.
The shipment will provide life-saving food assistance to more than 57,000 vulnerable people, including internally displaced, refugees, and communities, for the next three months, according to the UN World Food Programme (WFP).
The aid, consisting of yellow split peas, was officially handed over in Bamako on July 30 as part of Russia’s additional contribution to the WFP. Following the ceremony, participants visited a warehouse operated by the UN agency to review plans for distributing the humanitarian cargo.
The handover ceremony was attended by Malian government officials, WFP representatives, and members of the Russian diplomatic mission.
Russia’s сharge d’affaires in Mali, Bagrat Shinkuba, said Moscow continues to provide humanitarian assistance to friendly African nations both directly and through UN agencies. He added that the assistance is provided “without political conditions” and with respect for the sovereignty and national priorities of recipient states.
Malian Deputy Commissioner for Food Security Moussa Goita described the shipment as “an important humanitarian initiative and far from the first by Russia,” saying it reflected the growing partnership between Moscow and Bamako and demonstrated solidarity with the Malian people.
The West African nation has been battling a jihadist insurgency since 2012. The conflict, displacement, and climate shocks have fueled a humanitarian crisis. According to the WFP, around 1.6 million people face acute food insecurity, while more than 414,000 people are internally displaced.
Russia has previously provided humanitarian aid to Mali. In January 2024, Moscow supplied 25,000 metric tons of grain to the country, followed in December 2024 by a shipment of more than 65 metric tons of wheat delivered via the Guinean port of Conakry.
The delivery is part of Russia’s broader humanitarian outreach across Africa. Earlier this year, Moscow sent around 60 metric tons of emergency aid to cyclone-hit Madagascar and 29 metric tons of humanitarian supplies to Mozambique. In 2025, it also donated more than 1,600 metric tons of grain to Ethiopia under its ongoing food assistance program.
Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger – three military-led former French colonies – formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) in 2023 after severing defense ties with Paris, accusing France of failing to contain the insurgency. The three countries have since expanded cooperation with Russia.
Relations between Bamako and Paris have continued to deteriorate, with Malian officials accusing France of backing armed groups operating in the Sahel.
In May, broadcaster RTL, citing an unnamed French security source, reported that Paris was indirectly supporting Ukrainian personnel operating in Mali, who were allegedly cooperating with rebels in an attempt to overthrow the country’s military-led government.

Pope Leo XIV was welcomed to Assisi on Thursday by Fr. Marco Vianelli, Provincial Minister of the Friars Minor of Umbria and Sardinia, at the opening of the Pope's meeting with young people in Piazza Santa Maria degli Angeli, in front of the Basilica that houses the Porziuncola.

Young people as active participants, not passive spectators

Franciscan Youth Meeting 2026, which concludes today. "Thousands of young people from across Europe have gathered around the Porziuncola to share a journey of faith, hope, and fraternity."
Credible witnesses to the Gospel
In conclusion, the Provincial Minister once again thanked the Bishop of Rome for his presence, describing it as a sign of "encouragement and support in helping us become credible witnesses to the Gospel."

Pope in Assisi: Build a civilisation of love, not division
By Antonella Palermo
How can the spiritual legacy of Saint Francis of Assisi be lived out today? How can we embrace a spirit of service and welcome in a world increasingly shaped by oppression and consumerism? And how can we continue to trust a Church that is itself marked by crises and contradictions?
These were some of the questions put to the Pope today by three young people, who gave voice to concerns shared not only by their own generation, but by many others as well.
Pope Leo chose to begin his pastoral visit to the Umbrian town of Assisi by meeting young people at Santa Maria degli Angeli. Responding at length to each of their questions, he reiterated several key principles: religion must never be exploited for political purposes, while leadership should be liberating, responsible and inclusive.
Going against the tide: Healing memories and fostering reconciliation
Karolina, from Zagreb, was the first to speak. She asked how people can remain authentic disciples of Christ and share a living faith that does not remain confined within church walls.
In response, the Pope returned to the subject of war, recalling that Karolina comes from âa region of Europe that experienced war only thirty years ago, as well as the dangerous intertwining of religious affiliation and nationalism.â
The Franciscansâ long-standing commitment to dialogue in the region, he noted, has helped Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Muslims live together in peace. This, Pope Leo said, is the path that must continue to be followed.
âToday, being faithful to this tradition of closeness means going against the tide, working to heal memories and fostering reconciliation. Christians will increasingly be called to become peacemakers in societies tempted to exploit religion in conflicts between different identities.â
Misinformation and prejudice create fear; Christ opens the heart
To live as spiritual sons and daughters of Saint Francis of Assisi, the Pope stressed, means understanding the true meaning of Gospel radicalism.
It âis the opposite of fundamentalism: it does not make us blind and violent, but sensitive and attentive, always following Jesus and therefore humble and welcoming towards everyone. It is not easy, but it brings great joy.â
Following this path, the Pope suggested, sometimes means making uncomfortable or unfashionable choices, while resisting every attempt at manipulation.
âBearing witness to Christ therefore remains both fascinating and demanding, because it opens our minds and hearts beyond artificial boundariesâthat is, beyond the fears created by misinformation and the walls of prejudice.â
Technology makes us forget how to be together
Pope Leo then reflected on Saint Francisâ insight that poverty can bring people closer, even when they seem far apart.
He recalled what it means to be the Church: a home open to everyone, a community that listens and experiences the joy of fraternity. It is also a place where people rediscover the physical reality of being together, beyond the virtual world, and the value of silence, which âis the opposite of war, with its violence, shouting and cruelty.â
âDear young people, how beautiful it is to be together and âspeak about Godâ and, in His light, about life itself, in all its beauty, mystery and seriousness!â
âBear witness to this way of living wherever you go, especially at a time when technology is making us forget how to be together as people of flesh and blood.â
Making a lifelong commitment is a revolutionary act
Giovanni, from Bologna, asked the Pope how it is possible to give a wholehearted âyesâ to God in a world that often struggles to look beyond the immediate future or towards eternity.
He also asked what had helped Robert Prevost along his own vocational journey.

items.title: SIGNIS Africa renews its leadership
items.summary: SIGNIS Africa, the Catholic association for media practitioners, has ushered in a new board of directors. For the first time since its inception in 2001, women make up the majority of the board. The election took place on the sidelines of the SIGNIS World Congress happening in Kigali, Rwanda, from 03 August to 08 August 2026. Fr Fidele Mutabazi, a Rwandan priest of the Archdiocese of Kigali, was elected new SIGNIS Africa President. Read all
items.body_text:
SIGNIS Africa renews its leadership
Paul Samasumo â Kigali
Fr Mutabazi, the Managing Director of the Churchâs Kinyamateka Newspaper and Director of Communications for the Episcopal Conference of Rwanda, takes over from Nigerian priest and renowned academician, Professor Fr. Walter Chikwendu Ihejirika, who has completed his constitutional two terms. The new and complete SIGNIS Africa board also comprises the Chairperson of the Catholic Media Network Nairobi, Virginia Kabugu, who was elected as the new SIGNIS Africa Vice President.
Others elected to the seven-member board include Fr. Alexis Oudraogo of Burkina Faso. He was elected Secretary/Treasurer. Mozambican religious, Sr. Anastãncia Sebastãio Simbe FMA; Ms Clarice Azuatalam of Nigeria; Mr Kudakwashe Martin Matambo of Zimbabwe, and Miss Mwami Daka of Zambia are the other members.
Unprecedented and representative
Speaking after his election, Fr Mutabazi thanked the delegates and asked for their continued support. He commended the election as unprecedented and truly representative of the African reality in terms of geography and official languages spoken (English, French and Portuguese). He said he was happy that the Assembly of African delegates had not only given him a majority of women board members, but experts who, over and above their gender, were experienced media professionals and administrators.
Fr Mutabazi, who is the ad hoc chair of the ongoing SIGNIS World Congress Local Organising Committee (LOC), was praised by delegates for the meticulous attention to detail and efficiency displayed by the hosts in Kigali.
First time in Africa
The SIGNIS World Congress in Kigali has brought together over 200 Catholic journalists, media professionals, and communication experts from more than 40 countries across five continents. It is the first-ever SIGNIS World Congress to be hosted in Africa.
SIGNIS officially began as a worldwide association of communicators in November 2001. It was inaugurated in Rome during a joint congress through the merger of two older Catholic media organisations: OCIC (for cinema) and Unda (for radio and television), both of which were originally founded in 1928
